This document contains the Life Flight Network Flight and Ground Patient Care Guidelines. As guidelines,
they do not represent a standard of care. Every situation is unique. EMS is conducted in a stressful,
dynamic, and constantly changing environment. These guidelines cannot cover every type of injury,
illness, and complicating circumstance which may be encountered.
Situations will arise which are not covered within these guidelines or mitigate their usefulness, so use
them in conjunction with your training, experience, expertise, and always doing the right thing for the
patient. In such instances, you must function within your scope of practice and consider, when time and
circumstances permit, the use of other available resources, including 911 ground and on-line medical
control, to provide care commensurate with the patient’s injury and/or illness.
Available and relevant evidence was incorporated to support these guidelines. Where evidence was
lacking, we relied on best practices, expert advice, and consensus. These guidelines are reviewed on a
regular basis and updated when necessary to reflect advances in the art and science of critical care
transport.
For the State of Washington, these Patient Care Guidelines have been reviewed, approved, and adopted
by Dr. James Nania, Spokane County Medical Program Director. These protocols have also been
reviewed and approved by the Washington State Department of Health, Office of EMS with the exception
of protocols for non-EMS providers and skills and procedures that are outside the approved skills and
procedures for EMS providers. See the WA State approved skills and procedures for certified providers:
https://www.doh.wa.gov/Portals/1/Documents/Pubs/530173.pdf
As the Life Flight Network Medical Director and supervising physician, I approve these Patient Care
Guidelines and authorize their use by all Life Flight Network Flight Nurses, Flight Paramedics, Flight
Respiratory Therapists, Ground Nurses, Ground Paramedics, and Ground EMTs operating within their
scope of practice.
Matthew Conklin, MD
Life Flight Network Medical Director
Effective Date: 2/10/2026

Licensed and/or certified medical personnel providing patient care on behalf of Life Flight Network must
have a thorough knowledge of applicable state scopes of practice. Under no circumstances will patient
care exceed the scope of practice, training, or competency of an individual.
The Oregon Medical Board, Washington State Department of Health, Montana Board of Medical
Examiners, the Idaho EMS Physician Commission, and Hawaii Medical Board are responsible for the
scope of practice of Emergency Medical Service Providers as well as the requirements and duties of
these providers’ supervising physicians (EMS Medical Directors) in their respective state.
To view the complete Scope of Practice, see:
• Oregon Administrative Rule (OAR) 847-035-0030.
• Washington Administrative Code (WAC): 246-976-182
• Administrative Code of Montana (ACM): 24.156.2771
• Idaho EMSPC Scope of Practice 2020-1 Appendix
• Hawaii Revised Statues (HRS) §16-85-59
Each EMS Provider can perform the procedures of each lower-level certification plus those listed in their
certification level.
Registered Nurses (RN) may legally administer any medication or blood product within their scope of
practice and ordered via protocol, standing order, verbal order, or written order. They may also perform
any skill and/or procedure contained within these guidelines. CFRN Montana nurses get a critical care
endorsement which allows them to function as an EMR equivalent.
Paramedics (PM) may legally administer any medication contained within these guidelines provided the
medication is in their state-specific scope of practice and the medication is administered in accordance
with these guidelines. Refer to the table below for further information by state.
• In Washington, paramedics may transport patients with medications infusing if a department-
approved Medical Program Director (MPD) protocol is in place and providers have completed
department-approved MPD supplementary training on the medication and protocol.
Authorized medications and routes for paramedic personnel are identified in this document.
• In Oregon and Idaho, paramedics may administer any medication not contained in these
guidelines only when they receive an order from a physician, the medication is legally within
their scope of practice, additional training has been provided as approved by LFN’s Medical
Directors, and where the additional training is documented in the employee’s education
record. In the case of uncommon medications for which the paramedic has no training, the
Flight Nurse will be responsible for the administration and infusions.
Respiratory Therapists in Washington may provide treatment as defined by Scope of Practice
regulations (RCW 18.89.040). The interpretation of these regulations by the Executive Director of
Respiratory Therapists for respiratory care practitioner’s limits medication administration to agents
related to respiratory care.
Surgical cricothyrotomies and chest tubes are not in scope of practice, but our interpretation is needle
thoracostomies and placement of intraosseous lines are in scope, provided additional training has been
provided as approved by LFN’s Medical Directors and where the additional training is documented in the
employee’s education record. Intraosseous lines are not in the scope of practice in Oregon.

guidelines.title: Basic Approach to All Patient Contacts

blocks.text:
SAFETY IS OUR #1 PRIORITY! IT WILL TAKE PRECEDENCE OVER ALL OTHER CONCERNS!
1. All care shall be performed per these PCGs, except in rare cases where the situation precludes
adherence.
a. Any care not delineated by these PCGs requires documentation of medical decision making to
support provider decisions and care
b. These guidelines serve as a starting point for all patient care. Sound judgement and the best
interests of the patient should always prevail
2. Air medical transport provides speed of transport and improved patient access to any necessary
advanced procedures.  Ensure you and your team are At The Ready to provide these services.
Lifesaving interventions delivered too late do not improve survival.
3. Time at the base is time on shift at the service to our communities.  In the absence of patient calls
and following the completion of essential daily duties, you must prioritize sleep / rest until confident
you will be able to complete the remainder of your shift with sequential calls.

pediatric emergency, or other, benefit from resources at a tertiary care facility.  After brief initial
stabilization care, you shall expedite air transport. No patient is too unstable for air transport.
a. The assumption is the patient will otherwise succumb to their injuries or illness without
transport
b. In the case of a STEMI with arrest, if a mechanical CPR device is not available, a shorter
duration of suboptimal CPR is preferred to a longer duration of optimal CPR as CPR alone is
not indefinitely sustaining. The goal is rapid delivery to a center which can address or reverse
the cause of the condition
c. See destination determination for further information
5. Use personal protective equipment (PPE) for patient care. An N95 mask is required when caring for
any patient with pneumonia, meningitis, tuberculosis, fever, shortness of breath of unknown etiology,
or sepsis. Patients under investigation (PUI) for COVID-19 require full PPE.
6. End tidal CO2 (ETCO2) is required to be continuously monitored in the following patients:
a. All patients with an advanced airway
b. Patients with respiratory compromise, altered level of consciousness, and/or those receiving
sedatives and/or narcotics
c. All patients receiving ketamine regardless of dose or indication
7. Advanced airway transfers: disconnect ventilator/BVETT if tolerated; verify ETT/SGA securement in
commercial holder prior to movement; confirm placement with ETCO₂ immediately after each
transfer to prevent risk of unplanned extubation.
8. When practical and possible, obtain written consent from the patient before initiating any procedure,
including the administration of blood products.

All Patient Contacts
9. When it is known that the transport will require handoff to a second LFN crew, obtain written orders
for any medications and treatment parameters from the sending provider, when practicable and
possible.
10. The Handtevy resuscitation system is the approved reference for pediatric resuscitation. A length-
based resuscitation tape may be utilized for pediatric weight estimation.
11. Pediatric medication dosages should not exceed maximum single or total adult dose.
12. Pediatric patients are defined by CAMTS as < 18 years old. However, most patients with any evidence
of secondary sexual characteristics (pubic, axillary, facial hair, and/or breast development) may be
treated per adult guidelines.
a. Epinephrine, norepinephrine, dopamine, fentanyl, and midazolam infusions should be weight
based for all pediatric patients regardless of weight.
b. Pediatric IV push doses of epinephrine should be dosed AND documented in mL/kg.
c.  If transferring a patient to a pediatric ICU, make every effort to contact the receiving physician
prior to transport
13. Pediatric equipment formulas (*with an appropriately sized ETT):
a. ETT size: (Age + 16) / 4
i. Subtract 0.5 for cuffed ETT
b. NG/OG/Foley size: 2x ETT* size
c. ETT Depth: 3x ETT* size
d. Chest tube: 4x ETT* size
14. Pediatric Fluid Guidelines
a. Use D5NS for maintenance fluids
i. If D5 ½ NS is already initiated, switch to D5NS.
b. NS or LR may be used if glucose is contraindicated (head injury, diabetes/hyperglycemia), or if
D5NS is unavailable
c. For infants ≤ 28 days old, D10 may be used as an alternative to D5NS (rather than NS) for
maintenance fluids.
i. LR is contraindicated in this patient population
d. Do NOT give dextrose-containing solutions as a bolus, except when treating hypoglycemia
according to the appropriate guideline.
e. Pediatric maintenance fluid rate formulas:
i. <10 kg : 4 mL/kg
ii. 10 – 20 kg : 40 mL + 2 mL/kg for every kg > 10
iii. >20 kg body weight: 60 + 1 mL/kg for every kg > 20 kg
15. All patients presenting with neurological symptoms (e.g., CVA, AMS, seizure, etc.) should have
ongoing neurological assessment performed and documented at least q 15 minutes.
16. Whether a scene call or interfacility transfer, appropriate primary medical equipment should be taken
from the aircraft to the patient’s location. Consider your environment, as not all situations require all
equipment.

All Patient Contacts
17.  All medical crew members will have a thorough knowledge of each medication in our formulary.
Providers may decrease the dosage or prolong the administration intervals of any medication with
sedative properties when doing so would decrease adverse effects and still likely obtain the clinical
goal.
a. When administering medications at doses that are outside of this guideline, you must
document your reasoning along with a physical assessment that is related to pain and/or
sedation with pain and/or RASS scores.
18.  During handoffs at sending and receiving facilities, coordinate changing of infusions between pumps
to minimize interruptions of any critical infusions.
a. To minimize bedside time during STEMI transfers, heparin, and nitroglycerin infusions may be
clamped and pumps restarted after loading/lifting
19. It is expected that clinicians are familiar with the skills needed to perform advanced procedures.
Regardless of who actually performs the procedure, the second crew member is expected to assist
whenever feasible.
20.  Start a large bore IV with LR or saline lock as appropriate. For vasoactive medications, central lines
are preferable, but a good patent peripheral IV is acceptable.
a. Document IV site assessment with vasoactive medications q 15 minutes
b. Consider placing an IO, if vascular access is in question
i. The risk of ischemic necrosis secondary to extravasation is the same, regardless of
which vasoactive medication is utilized
c. Any If necessary and appropriate, any medication or fluid suitable for IV administration,
including blood, may be administered via an IO
21.  All syringes containing medications which are not immediately administered (such as push dose
epinephrine) will be labeled with the medication name and concentration.
a. Only draw up the amount of medication you intend to administer into your syringe.
22. Systolic blood pressure (SBP) goals most patients should be a normal SBP, with a few exceptions
which are listed below. Patients being outside of the targeted range may not require immediate
treatment but should be continuously monitored by the crew (i.e., a vasopressor may not be required
before trialing fluid boluses).
a. Normal SBP:
i. Adults: ranges from 90 – 120 mmHg
ii. Children < 10 years old: > 90 + (age x2) mmHg
b. Hypotensive patients:
i. Adults and children: SBP > 90 mmHg
c. Hemorrhagic Shock
i. Adults and children ≥ 10 years: SBP 80 – 90 mmHg or presence of a radial pulse
ii. Children < 10 years: SBP > 80 mmHg or presence of a brachial pulse
d. Evidence of head injury:
i. Adults and children ≥ 10 years: SBP 110 mmHg
ii. Children < 10 years: SBP > 90 + (age x2) mmHg
23. Vital Sign Requirements:
a. Vital signs are required to be transmitted from the monitor to the ePCR via the cloud

All Patient Contacts
b. Obtain and document baseline vital signs (BP, HR, RR, SpO2,ETCO2) and GCS on all patients.
i. Include baseline and ongoing ETCO2 for patients with any managed airway
c. Non-intubated patients:  ETCO2 NC documentation is required for patients receiving multiple
doses of pain medications, any amount of ketamine, and those receiving analgesia infusions
or use of sedatives.
d. Q 5 min vitals (or more often as required) for scene calls or unstable transports. The term
“unstable "includes but is not limited to patients:
i. Requiring vasoactive medications (e.g., vasopressor(s), nitroglycerin, nicardipine,
etc…) blood products, and/or multiple fluid boluses for hemodynamic support.
ii. Performance of advanced procedures until vital signs stabilize.
e. Q 15 min vitals for stable transports
f. Q 30 min vitals for extended transports with a stable patient
24. Ventilator Documentation:
a. Ventilator settings and ongoing monitor data is required to be documented q 15 minutes
i. Q 30-minute checks are acceptable for stable transports that exceed 90 minutes and
when the patient’s oxygenation, ventilation, and hemodynamics are stable and
require minimal interventions or adjustments
b. Required documentation elements include:
i. Mode, Rate, VT or target VT, PIP, PEEP, & FiO2
ii. Exhaled tidal volume (VTe)
iii. Cstat (if used to obtain plateau pressure)
iv. Plateau pressure (if applicable)
• If Pplat ≤ 30, only one plateau pressure is required
• If Pplat > 30, document q 15 minutes or until ≤ 30
v. At least one ETT cuff pressure measurement is required
25. If you are transporting a patient with an existing arterial line or PA catheter, you should continue to
transduce and document the values in your ePCR.

guidelines.title: Basic Approach for BLS Transport Teams

blocks.text:
ADULT & PEDIATRIC:
1. If indicated, maintain an open airway through the use of:
• NPA/OPA
• Pharyngeal suctioning device
2. Maintain existing CPAP using a Flow-Safe II if patient is stable and current CPAP/PEEP
level is attainable with Flow-Safe II (usually ≤ 10 cmH2O)
3. Perform tracheobronchial tube suctioning PRN to maintain patency if patient has
tracheostomy tube
4. Transport stable patients with saline locks, urinary catheters, or in-dwelling vascular
devices as needed
5. Provide care for suspected shock
• Provide hemorrhage control
• Place patient supine
• Do not place in Trendelenburg position
6. Provide care for musculoskeletal injuries as needed
7. Assist an Advanced EMT, EMT-Intermediate, or Paramedic by:
• Assembling and priming IV fluid administration sets
• Opening, assembling, and uncapping preloaded medication syringes and vials
8. Assist a patient with administration of sublingual nitroglycerin and with metered dose
inhalers that have been previously prescribed by that patient’s personal physician and
are in the possession of the patient at the time the EMT is summoned to assist that
patient.
9. For patients requiring minimal control for patient or staff safety, place soft restraints as
needed if patient cannot be verbally calmed or redirected.
• Check and document circulation, motor, and sensation (CMS) initially and q 15
minutes on patients in restraints
• Violent patients require ALS transport
• If patient is placed in soft restraints, complete a QM report

1. If given concurrently, consider doses lower than would be utilized when giving either a
benzodiazepine or narcotic alone.
2. Treat pain with narcotics until symptoms improve before giving sedative/anxiolytic so as
to avoid excess sedation.

can result in sudden and unexpected sedation and respirator compromise.

medication with sedative properties when doing so would decrease adverse effects and
still likely to obtain the clinical goal.

pain and/or sedation with pain scales and/or RASS scores.

blocks.text: Combative Patient

6. Assessment Considerations:
a. Among the most difficult tasks in providing care during an adult behavioral
emergency is determining the etiologies of combative patients and treating
accordingly, be it medical, toxicological, or traumatic in nature.
b. Approximately two-thirds of behavioral emergency patients have a non-
psychiatric (organic) etiology:
i. Psychiatric (functional)
ii. Non-psychiatric (organic)
iii. Medical (CVA, hypoglycemia, increased ICP, meningitis, etc.)
iv. Toxicological
7. Consent may be obtained via:
a. Informed consent through discussion with the patient / family
b. Implied consent due to severe injuries or patient inability to demonstrate capacity
for medical decision making
c. Physician consent
d. Law Enforcement does not provide consent for procedures but can request
assistance with maintaining safety of patients in their custody.
8. If the patient has previously been sedated by sending providers, they may potentially lack
capacity for refusal of medical transport
a. You may need to rely on statements of consent given to providers prior to your
arrival
b. Consider contacting medical control
9. While rare, droperidol may cause dystonic symptoms, which is treated with diphenhydramine
a. Refer to diphenhydramine formulary entry for dosing
b. Dystonic reactions are hyperkinetic movements characterized by sustained or
intermittent, repetitive, patterned, tremulous, or jerky movements affecting the
extremities, face, neck, trunk, pelvis, or larynx.

blocks.text:
1. Continuous waveform capnography shall be monitored on all patients with an advanced airway in
place.
2. Monitor capnography via ETCO2 NC for all non-intubated patients with respiratory
compromise, with an altered level of consciousness, and those receiving sedation, narcotics, or
any combination of sedative medications and narcotics.
3. Initiate Rapid Sequence Induction when appropriate
a. The RSI checklist is required to be utilized for all intubations unless a crash airway
b. A bougie should be used as a stylet, especially for anterior airways
i. Adult bougie: ETT size ≥ 5.5 , noting the 5.5 is a tight fit
ii. Pediatric bougie: ETT size ≥3.5, noting the 3.5 is a tight fit
c. A stylet is required for ETTs ≤ 4.0 in patients where a Mac 3 or Mac 4 blade would be
appropriate.
d. The C-MAC should be used beginning with the first intubation attempt
4. All patients with an advanced airway must be placed on and transported via mechanical
ventilator, regardless of estimated transport time. This includes IFTs and scenes calls.
a. Transporting a patient with an advanced airway without use of the ventilator should be
reserved for equipment failure or other rare extenuating circumstances. This may include
excessive leaks with a supraglottic airway device that cannot be adequately addressed.
b. The reason for not utilizing the ventilator must be appropriately documented.
5. The ventilator should be taken into the sending facility when transporting a patient that is intubated
or receiving non-invasive ventilation,
a. Regardless of the patient’s reported respiratory status, the ventilator should always be
taken from the airport or other remote landing locations to the hospital, as patient
conditions frequently change.
b. When changing patients over to LFN’s ventilator, minimize time off the ventilator, without
PEEP, to prevent loss of recruitment.
6. In COVID-19, ARDS and similar pathology, higher ventilator rates/pressures and 100% FiO2 can
potentially harm lung tissue and cause O2 utilization beyond that available for completion of
transport; SpO2 can be maintained ≥ 87% if necessary.

1. All patients receiving sedatives require continuous monitoring of ECG, blood pressure,
HR, SpO2, ETCO2.
2. Pain and sedation meds should be reduced in patients with hypotension (while
aggressively treating the hypotension)
3. Clinicians may reduce the dose or increase timing interval of any medication in this
guideline, when doing so may reduce adverse effects while still likely to obtain the
clinical goal.
4. When administering medications at doses that are outside of this guideline you must
document your reasoning along with a physical assessment that is related to pain and/or
sedation with pain and/or RASS scores.
a. This should be a rare event.
5. Patients that are chemically paralyzed should NOT have RASS/CPOT scores
documented. Please document “Chemically Paralyzed” under the GCS qualifier.
a. Once the patient is no longer paralyzed, you should include RASS/CPOT score as
required by LFN documentation standards.
6. Chemically paralyzed patients may require doses at the higher end of the dose range
(blood pressure permitting) to ensure adequate sedation.
7. If blood pressure improves, give concurrent dose of lorazepam or midazolam to blunt
emergence phenomenon.
8. For excessive salivation post-ketamine administration administer atropine
a. Adult: 0.25 mg IV
b. Pedi: 0.01 mg/kg IV

3. Special Considerations and Malfunctions
• Cardiac Arrest
o Immediately perform CPR.
o IABP will automatically switch to pressure trigger, except in PEA.
▪ You must unplug the ECG leads so the pump does not sense R waves.
o There is no need to adjust the pump in the event of cardiac arrest. Treat the
patient as you normally would in cardiac arrest.
o If ROSC is achieved, remember to plug the ECG leads back into the pump once
PEA coverts. The pump will switch back to ECG triggers if/when it sees a
consistent ECG rhythm.
• Balloon Rupture
o “Gas Loss” alarm with blood in catheter tubing
o If blood is present in the gas line, immediately turn off the pump and alert the
sending physician for assessment and balloon removal
• Pump Failure
o If the IABP is off or non-functional for > 30 minutes, the IAB should be manually
inflated and deflated to prevent clot formation on the balloon using the steps
below.
o Ensure the receiving physician and dispatch are aware of the issue.
o Detach catheter extender from IAB catheter’s male luer fitting.
o If using a luer lock, attach the supplied 3-way stopcock and syringe to IAB
catheter’s male luer fitting.
o Aspirate to ensure blood is not returned through the extracorporeal tubing.
o Inflate IAB with 40 mL of air or helium an immediately aspirate
▪ Repeat q 5 minutes while IAB is inactive
o Once a functional IAB pump is available, remove the 3-way stopcock and syringe
and reattach IAB catheter’s male luer fitting to catheter extender and resume
pump.
• Gas Loss Alarm
o Check the patient.
o Utilize HELP button on the alarm screen to walk through potential
causes/solutions.
o Potential causes:
▪ Balloon rupture (check for blood/black rust in tubing)
▪ Tubing disconnect
▪ Patient coughing
▪ Condensation in tubing
▪ Tachycardia/febrile

1. Medical Management:
• In the event of cardiac arrest:
o Treat per Basic Life Support and Cardiac Arrest: Medical guidelines
o Reduce P-level to 2
o If ROSC is obtained, verify pulsatile motor current and appropriate placement
signal waveforms before returning to previous P-level
• Maintaining optimal patient hemodynamic status and correct Impella position are two
key factors in managing patients supported with the Impella® System during transport.
• Steps should be taken to eliminate or minimize any aspect of the transport that might
adversely affect these two factors.
• Initial settings will have been ordered and established by a physician.
o After these settings have been made, the Impella system is fully automated.
• As the Impella decreases overall workload of the heart, native heart function may be
decreased in patients on the Impella system.
o Treat the mean arterial pressure (MAP) rather than the systolic and diastolic
pressures (target MAP ≥ 65)
o Contact sending or receiving physician for orders to change P level or add
vasopressors to maintain MAP
o Alarms to be set and on at all times
2. Prior to Transport:
• Confirm battery is fully charged.
o Temporarily unplug Impella Controller to assure battery is operational. When fully
charged, the battery provides 60 minutes of operation
o Minimize time the Impella unit is unplugged from AC power to ensure adequate
battery life for unforeseen power losses
• Confirm purge fluid is dextrose in water (usually D5W) plus heparin 25-50 units/mL or
sodium bicarbonate 25-50 mEq/L
o Consider obtaining a backup purge cassette from sending facility; return with
controller if unused
o Ensure there is no air in the bag; remove if present
o Ensure there is ≥ 500 mL purge fluid remaining to complete the transport
o If not, change the purge fluid bag prior to leaving the sending facility

Contraindications
Cardiogenic shock
Mural thrombus in left ventricle
Advanced heart failure
Mechanical aortic valve or heart
Unstable patient requiring emergency constrictive device
Aortic valve stenosis/calcification cardiac catheterization/protected PCI
Before, during or after open-heart surgery or
Moderate to severe aortic insufficiency cardiac catheterization

24/7 Abiomed Clinical Support Line: 1-800-422-8666
Medical Management:
In the event of cardiac arrest:
Treat per Basic Life Support and Cardiac Arrest: Medical guidelines
Reduce P-level to 2
If ROSC is obtained, verify pulsatile motor current and appropriate placement signal waveforms before returning to previous P-level
Maintaining optimal patient hemodynamic status and correct Impella position are two key factors in managing patients supported with the Impella® System during transport.
Steps should be taken to eliminate or minimize any aspect of the transport that might adversely affect these two factors.
Initial settings will have been ordered and established by a physician.
After these settings have been made, the Impella system is fully automated.
As the Impella decreases overall workload of the heart, native heart function may be decreased in patients on the Impella system.
Treat the mean arterial pressure (MAP) rather than the systolic and diastolic pressures (target MAP ≥ 65)
Contact sending or receiving physician for orders to change P level or add vasopressors to maintain MAP
Alarms to be set and on at all times
Prior to Transport:
Confirm battery is fully charged.
Temporarily unplug Impella Controller to assure battery is operational. When fully charged, the battery provides 60 minutes of operation
Minimize time the Impella unit is unplugged from AC power to ensure adequate battery life for unforeseen power losses
Confirm purge fluid is dextrose in water (usually D5W) plus heparin 25-50 units/mL or
sodium bicarbonate 25-50 mEq/L
Consider obtaining a backup purge cassette from sending facility; return with controller if unused
Ensure there is no air in the bag; remove if present
Ensure there is ≥ 500 mL purge fluid remaining to complete the transport
If not, change the purge fluid bag prior to leaving the sending facility
Confirm Impella placement via the Impella console by observing all of the following:
Red placement signal, which should appear as an aortic waveform,
LV placement signal, which should appear as a ventricular waveform, AND
Green motor current, which should be pulsatile
If there is any evidence of catheter migration, position must be confirmed and/or catheter repositioned via echocardiogram (physician only)
For an Impella placed via the femoral artery, consider placing a knee immobilizer on the side of the catheter to prevent hip flexion and catheter migration
Confirm the repositioning unit is secured to the patient with two forward facing sutures in the blue suture pad.
Note and document the catheter length at the insertion site
Ensure the Tuohy lock is locked and tightened (clockwise) so the catheter does not migrate.
DO NOT overtighten
Note appearance of Impella insertion site
No blood should be seen in the purge fluid tubing or flush port
Notify the sending or receiving physician if blood is present
Confirm distal pulses on side of Impella insertion
Ensure angle matching is maintained
Assess for site bleeding and/or hematoma
Note Impella settings, size of device (i.e., CP, 5.5, RP, and RP Flex), and any complications during insertion.
Consider placing Zoll multi-function pads, if appropriate
Maintain head of bed at 30 degrees or less
Prior to any movement of the patient, ensure the Impella catheter is secured, and the Connector Cable and IV lines are clear of any obstacles or kinking
Loading and unloading of the Impella console at the referring and receiving facilities are under the direction of LFN personnel
After loading the Impella Controller, secure with FAA approved securing straps and ensure Impella Controller is plugged into aircraft power

Document vitals, Impella flow rate (liters/min), purge pressure and proper catheter position (placement signal and motor current) q 15 minutes
Assess catheter insertion site appearance, catheter position (length) and distal pulses on side of Impella insertion before and after each move and PRN

The catheter cannot be repositioned by the flight crew during transport.
The automated purge system will run between 2-30 mL/hr to maintain a purge pressure between 300-1100 mmHg
Alarms can be temporarily silence by pressing the Mute Alarm button
Alarm will not re-sound if condition causing alarm has been corrected

Medical Management (continued)
o Defibrillation, cardioversion, or pacing are all acceptable, if necessary:
▪ Do NOT place pads over pump.
▪ Anterior/posterior pad placement is acceptable.
▪ Do NOT stop VAD to deliver the shock.
o VADs can be pulsatile or non-pulsatile (continuous flow)
▪ Patient may or may not have a palpable pulse.
▪ Taking a BP with an automatic BP cuff or stethoscope and cuff is
unreliable.
▪ Doppler is the best way to obtain BP.
▪ Pulse oximetry readings may not be accurate due to weak pulses.
o If LVAD function cannot be restored, and:
▪ The patient is unresponsive, AND
▪ Has signs of poor perfusion and ETCO2 <20 mmHg, AND
▪ There are no contraindications from family or POLST
▪ CPR IS INDICATED
• If the patient is hypovolemic, treat per Cardiogenic Shock.
o The goal is to maintain MAP > 50 mmHg
• Auscultate over the pump, located at the lower left rib margin of the anterior chest.
o A distinct ‘hum’ will be heard if device is functioning.
• When assessing/treating patient, do not cut, twist, or bend the driveline.
• When loading patient, make sure the driveline does not get pulled or kinked and the
controller and battery packs are close to the patient and not dangling off side of
stretcher.
• When transporting patient, have emergency travel pack with patient at all times, which
contains:
o Extra batteries
o Backup controller
o VAD coordinator’s emergency contact number
2. Troubleshooting
• If VAD is alarming, ensure driveline and two sources of power (dual batteries or AC power)
are connected to the system controller.
o If alarms continue, change the batteries.
o DO NOT remove both batteries at the same time or pump will stop.
• If pump is stopped, replace both batteries with two charged batteries.
o If pump does not restart, change the controller.
• If using AC power, ensure inverter in aircraft or ambulance is on.
• In event of pump failure, contact the VAD coordinator for guidance and instruction.
• Listen to concerns from patient and family members who have received device specific
training.
o Allow them to manage device and transport family ‘LVAD expert’ with the patient
when possible

3. Background Information
• Most of the areas served by LFN use one of two LVADs.
o Heartmate II or HeartWare
• The main difference between the two is how they connect to the left ventricle.
o Blood flows via the normal path through the heart until it reaches the left
ventricle.
o The implanted LVAD has a cannula or pump placed in the apex of the heart which
drains blood from the left ventricle into the system pump.
o The pump then drives the blood into the ascending aorta.
o The driveline exits the abdominal wall and connects the internal pump to the
external controller.
o The controller is the brains of the device and controls the power to the pump,
manages the pump speed, and reports alarms and other operating parameters to
the user.
• The controller is connected to an electrical source.
o Two batteries or an AC power unit.
• LVAD patients are typically on anticoagulation medications and complications usually
result from anticoagulation (GI or intracranial bleeds) or pump thrombus (CVAs or pump
thrombosis).

1. If intubated, the goal of mechanical ventilation is to maintain adequate oxygenation and
ventilation while minimizing elevated airway pressures.

2. You may exceed the max dose if the patient remains hypotensive despite adequate fluid
resuscitation and the initiation of a second vasopressor.

ADULT and PEDIATRIC:
1. The displayed joule setting in Handtevy may not exactly match the calculated dose as
the displayed values are rounded to the closest appropriate joule level that can be
selected on the Zoll X-Series.
2. Before treating heart rate with medications, rule out other causes of tachycardia (e.g.,
sepsis, trauma, fever) and treat as needed.
3. All patients receiving medications within this guideline must have defibrillation pads in
place
4. Use caution when administering adenosine to patients with asthma
5. There is controversy between using beta blockers versus calcium channel blockers
a. In general, if known, treat with the same class medication the patient takes orally
6. Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome is a disorder due to a specific type of problem with the
electrical system of the heart involving an accessory pathway able to conduct electrical
current between the atria and the ventricles, thus bypassing the atrioventricular node.
a. AV node blockers should be avoided in atrial fibrillation and atrial flutter with
WPW or history of it; this includes adenosine, diltiazem, verapamil, other calcium
channel blockers, and beta blockers
i. They can exacerbate the syndrome by blocking the heart's normal
electrical pathway potentially leading to unstable ventricular arrhythmias
b. The classic ECG pattern of preexcitation in sinus rhythm is characterized by a
fusion between conduction via the accessory pathway and the normal AV
node/His-Purkinje system
i. The PR interval is short (less than 0.12 seconds) due to rapid AV
conduction through the accessory pathway and bypass of the AV nod
ii. The QRS complex consists of fusion between early and direct ventricular
myocardial activation caused by preexcitation and the later ventricular
activation resulting from transmission through the AV node and the
infranodal conduction system to the ventricles
iii. While beginning earlier than expected, the initial part of ventricular
activation is slow, and the upstroke of the QRS complex is slurred because
of slow muscle-fiber-to-muscle-fiber conduction.
1. This is known as a delta wave (red arrows on ECG below)

blocks.text:
ADULT and PEDIATRIC:
1. About 75% of patients will experience symptoms within one hour, and 90% within 12
hours of surfacing.
2. Type I decompression sickness (mild): typically affects the musculoskeletal, cutaneous,
and lymphatic systems leading to join pain (elbow and shoulder more often than knee
and hip), pruritus of the upper torso, lymphadenopathy, and edema.
3. Type II decompression sickness (more severe): involves the nervous and pulmonary
systems.
a. Spinal cord symptoms include weakness, paresthesia, and paraplegia, including
loss of bladder control.
b. Cerebral manifestations include memory loss, ataxia, visual disturbances and
changes in personality, speech and affect.
c. Pulmonary symptoms due to pulmonary venous gas emboli include chest pain,
wheezing, dyspnea, cough, circulatory collapse and death.

• Ventilatory support is of primary importance in drowning patients.
• Place on 100% oxygen, intubate if needed; see Rapid Sequence Induction
o ETT placement is preferred for airway management
• Suction airway PRN
o If foam is present during resuscitation, PPV is preferred to “push” foam down
rather than suctioning6
• Initiate resuscitation if:
o The patient was submerged < 30 minutes, OR
o The patient was submerged for 30 – 60 minutes AND if any of the following are
present:
▪ Water temperature < 5° C (41° F)
▪ Possibility of entrapment in an underwater air pocket
▪ Water temperature 5 – 20° C (41 – 68° F) and the patient had been
swimming on the surface for a prolonged period before drowning
▪ Crew discretion
• Target normothermic temperature (36 – 37.5° C) after ROSC in order to provide cerebral
protection.

2. Hypothermia may be protective in drowning, however, unless the water is extremely cold
(<5°C/41°F), cooling is usually not rapid enough to provide cerebral protection.

protection if the patient was seen on the surface for a prolonged period prior to
submersion or a car into the water with question of an air pocket, etc.

(better potential) vs. dead and then cold (poor potential).

submersion (cough, shortness of breath, hypoxia) should be transported.

death over ensuing hours to days (previously called secondary drowning, although
this term is no longer used).

blocks.text: Drowning

5. Hypoxemia is the most life-threating consequence of near drowning for both salt and
fresh water.
a. Fresh water alters the composition of pulmonary surfactant in the alveoli,
changing their surface tension and leading to alveolar collapse.
b. Saltwater causes protein-rich fluid to extravasate into the alveoli, causing
surfactant to wash out.
c. Both types of water end with V/Q mismatch, intrapulmonary shunting, and
decrease compliance.
6. A key clinical pitfall in the management of the drowning patient is to suction the foam
that comes up from the lungs into the oral cavity during resuscitation.
a. This is often intuitive as we typically suction blood, emesis, or anything else that
could potentially hinder oxygen exchange.
b. Foam in drowning is a result of lung surfactant mixed with water that bubbles up
like soap and water.
c. It is non-toxic and contains lung surfactant that patients’ lungs need.
d. As such it should not be suctioned, as such attempts will delay definitive airway
management.
e. Rather, positive pressure ventilation should be used to push the foam back down
into the lungs.
f. Foam in the upper airway is an indication for endotracheal intubation.
7. As soiling the airway with emesis is common in drowning, the resuscitation team should
be prepared to perform suction assisted laryngoscopy airway decontamination (SALAD).
a. This technique is used to prevent airway soiling during laryngoscopy as a result of
aspirated emesis.
b. SALAD involves using a rigid suction catheter as a sort of tongue depressor to
allow the laryngoscope blade to be placed in the ideal position
c. The suction catheter is then used to decontaminate the proximal esophagus and
stays pinned in the left corner of the patient’s oral cavity.
d. Antiemetics, which may prevent soiling of the airway from emesis, are reasonable
to administer during the resuscitation of the drowning patient.

blocks.text:
ADULT & PEDIATRIC:
• Wash the bite with soap and water and cover the area with a clean, moist dressing to
minimize swelling and discomfort.
• Remove all rings, watches, and constrictive clothing in case of swelling.
• Mark the leading (proximal) edge plus measure the circumference at 10cm and 20cm
proximal to the bite to allow for monitoring of progression in erythema or size.
• Immobilize the bitten extremity and keep it lower than the heart.
• Do not apply a tourniquet, cut the wound, suck out the venom, apply ice or immerse in
cold water.
• Do not allow bystanders to apply an electric shock which has been advocated by some
as beneficial.
• Treatment may cause allergic reactions.
• Patients with possible envenomation but without symptoms should be observed closely
and not treated unless symptoms develop.

ADULT and PEDIATRIC:
1. There are two antivenin products approved for use in the US: Crotalidae Polyvalent
Immune Fab (CroFab®) and Crotalidae Immune F(ab’)2 (Anavip®).
a. Prehospital use of antivenin should be weighed against availability (local hospital
willing to provide antivenin) and the delay required to obtain the medication from
the facility.
b. In general, prehospital use should be considered only in cases when hospital
arrival time will be more than two hours after the bite.
c. See LFN formulary for mixing and administration information.
d. If allergic reaction or anaphylaxis develop, stop the infusion, see Anaphylaxis and
Allergic Reaction.
2. Non-envenomation (i.e., dry bite), occurs in approximately 10% of rattlesnake bites.
3. A severe envenomation may require > 10 vials of antivenom.
a. Dosing is based on severity rather than patient weight, thus repeat dosing may be
required
4. Snakebites rarely have two obvious fang marks and venom may injected even in the
absence of any visible markings.
a. Most snakes are non-venomous, however venomous snakes have a few
specific physical traits.

ADULT & PEDIATRIC:
• If the hypothermic patients has no signs of life, begin CPR, including airway management
immediately
• For MILD hypothermia begin passive rewarming
o Move patient to a warm environment.
o Remove wet clothing.
o Provide blankets, especially around head.
• For MODERATE to SEVERE hypothermia, begin active rewarming:
o Apply wrapped hot packed to axilla, neck, and groin.
• If frostbite is present:
o Place gauze between any involved fingers and/or toes. Cover with dry, bulky sterile
dressings.
o Do not attempt re-warming if there is a possibility of re-freezing of area.
o Do not rub the affected area.

blocks.text:
ADULT and PEDIATRIC:
1. Most frostbite thaws spontaneously and should be allowed to do so if rapid rewarming
cannot be readily achieved. However, this should be done slowly, so keep the injured
tissue away from heat sources during transport. The most effective method is to rewarm
the area quickly.
2. There is some evidence of benefit from intra-arterial thrombolytic therapy. Contact
OLMC and consider transport to a facility with the capability of performing this
treatment.
3. Rewarming (usually not initiated by LFN) is accomplished by immersing the affected area
in a tub of gently re-circulating water at 37° – 39°C (98.6° - 102.2°F).
a. Thawing usually takes approx. 30 min.
b. Rectal/Core temperature <30°C (86°F) results in increased risk of ventricular
dysrhythmias/VF.
4. Avoid intubation which can result in fatal arrhythmias. The patient may maintain a very
low respiratory rate, which can seem undetectable. Respiratory status can improve with
further warming.
5. Handle patient gently, keep horizontal (if able), and limit movement of extremities.
6. Extremes of age and antihypertensive medications may increase the risk of hypothermia.
7. Medications may not be effective if core temperature is <30°C (86°F)
8. Hypothermic patients may be candidates for ECMO for cardiopulmonary bypass. Notify
receiving hospital as soon as possible.
9. HYPOTHERMIA:
a. Mild:
i. Normal body temperature 35-32.1°C (95-89.8°F); conscious, shivering.
b. Moderate:
i. 32°-28°C (89.7°-82.5°F); impaired consciousness, not shivering.
c. Severe:
i. <28°C (82.4°F); unconscious, not shivering, V/S deteriorating.

blocks.text:
Hypothermia &
Frost Bite

10. FROSTBITE:
a. Superficial:
i. Burning, numbness, tingling, itching or cold sensation.
ii. Erythema and edema, white or yellow, firm plaque progressing to vesicles
with clear or milky fluid.
b. Deep:
i. Sensation is initially decreased then completely lost.
ii. Tissue may have swelling and blood-filled blisters progressing to necrosis
extending into the muscle and bone.
iii. There is significant pain as the areas are rewarmed and blood flow
reestablished.
iv. Tissue may initially appear deceptively healthy.
v. Significant pain and final tissue damage evolve over time.
vi. Final amount of tissue damage is proportional to the time it remains
frozen, not to the absolute temperature to which it was exposed.

ADULT:
• ALL BLS and ALS Treatments Above
• Significant pain and nausea contributes to hypertension and tachycardia and should be
managed aggressively.
o See pain management and/or nausea & vomiting
• Vital Sign Targets:
o Aortic dissection: HR < 60 AND SBP < 120
o Aortic ruptures: SBP > 80 (permissive hypotension)
If HR and/or SBP are outside of targets, initiate one of the following beta blockers:
• Esmolol infusion via IV pump, is the preferred first line agent (when available), and
should be obtained from the sending facility if it would not cause a delay in transport
o Dosing: (see dosing chart below)
1. Administer initial 500 mcg/kg bolus over 60 seconds, then initiate
infusion at 50 mcg/kg/min
2. If, after 4 minutes, vital signs are still above target, repeat 500 mcg/kg
bolus over 60 seconds, and increase infusion to 100 mcg/kg/min
3. If, after 4 minutes, vital signs are still above target, repeat 500 mcg/kg
bolus over 60 seconds, and increase infusion to 150 mcg/kg/min
4. Continue to titrate in 50 mcg/kg/min increments q 4 min without a re-
bolus until target HR and SBP are met or max rate of 300 mcg/kg/min has
been met

ADULT and PEDIATRIC:
1. Pain control is an important modifier of both HR and BP and should be addressed early.
2. Monitor urine output and patient mentation to assess perfusion. Assess variation in
blood pressure and heart rate in all extremities (right vs left / upper vs lower).
3. Any mismatch noticed may help to gauge progression of the disease.
4. It is imperative to ensure that you will have enough medication to last the entire
transport.
5. Aortic injury (trauma) and aortic dissection (medical) are different entities, but treatment
of associated tachycardia and hypertension is the same.
6. With traumatic aortic injury, blood is usually contained in a mediastinal hematoma, as a
free rupture is normally fatal within minutes without surgical intervention.
a. Therefore, tachycardia and persistent or recurrent hypotension, especially in the
absence of medical treatment (e.g., esmolol, nicardipine), is usually due to blood
loss from an alternative site.
b. Treat as needed with fluids and/or blood, see Blood Product Administration.
7. Impulse therapy recognizes the damage to the artery from both the pressure as well as
the rate of pulsation.
a. Vasodilators can cause reflex tachycardia. Therefore, the guidance is to start with
a beta blocker and then give further vasodilator, such as nicardipine to achieve
goal blood pressure.

• All BLS Treatments Above

increased mortality
• If patient is intubated, place on ventilator and maintain ETCO2 at 35 – 45.

• Monitor for signs of increased intracranial pressure/herniation 1
• If signs of herniation are present, intubate per Rapid Sequence Induction (RSI)
• In order to maintain adequate cerebral blood flow, hypotension should be managed with
fluid resuscitation and vasopressors as needed to maintain SBP> 110 or SBP> 90 + (2 x age in
years) in pediatric patients3

blocks.text:
ADULT and PEDIATRIC:
1. Signs and Symptoms of herniation:
a. In patients with an initial GCS ≤ 8, a decrease in the GCS of more than two points.
b. A unilateral, dilated pupil is the hallmark sign of herniation. Progresses to bilateral
and fixed as herniation worsens.
c. Decerebrate/extensor posturing.
d. Cushing reflex (hypertension, bradycardia, irregular respirations/apnea)
e. Hemiparesis on side opposite the dilated pupil
2. The ETCO2 goal for all patients with known or suspected head injuries, including those with
suspected herniation is 35 – 40 mmHg. Hyperventilation to obtain lower ETCO2 goals has not
been shown to improve patient outcomes.
3. Note that this target BP is lower than the target SBP of 140 – 150 when treating hypertensive
patients with nicardipine and/or labetalol.
a. When lowering BP in hypertensive patients, it is harmful to overshoot and cause
hypotension.

ADULT and PEDIATRIC:
1. Hypokalemia:
a. Indications for IV potassium replacement include:
i. Potassium < 2.5, OR
ii. Potassium < 3.0, with one or more of the following:
• Cardiac irritability/dysrhythmias
• Cardiac ischemia/infarction
• Severe weakness, hypoventilation, or paralysis
• Recent administration of potassium wasting diuretics
• Digoxin administration (especially digoxin toxicity) or other arrhythmias
• As a component of DKA management (following correction of acidosis)
2. Hyperkalemia:
a. It is imperative to ask at the sending hospital if a repeat potassium level was drawn
and/or if hyperkalemia treatment was done
i. We do not carry insulin, so reversal needs to be done at the sending hospital
b. Treatment should be provided if potassium level is ≥ 6 mEq/L, even if there are no
ECG changes
i. However, in the absence of ECG changes, calcium is usually not indicated
c. Potassium levels < 6 mEq/L rarely requires acute treatment
d. Presume hyperkalemia is present in at risk patients (e.g., history of renal failure,
rhabdomyolysis, etc…) in cardiac arrest or those with ECG changes consistent with
hyperkalemia
e. In the absence of ECG changes or acute renal failure, confirm hyperkalemia prior to
transport, when possible
f. Hyperkalemia associated with DKA will correct with fluids and insulin therapy
i. Do not administer sodium bicarbonate to patients in DKA
g. Dialysis is the definitive treatment of choice for the removal of potassium, especially
in patients with moderate to severe renal failure
h. A single dose of Sodium Polystyrene Sulfonate (Kayexalate) is rarely effective and
can cause bowel obstruction or fatal ileus. Use should be limited to patients with
potentially life-threatening hyperkalemia when dialysis is not readily available.
i. Contraindicated in postoperative patients, patients with ileus or large/small
bowel obstruction, patients receiving opioids and those with bowel disease
such as ulcerative colitis or Clostridium difficile
• Adults: 30 grams PO/PR
• Pediatric: 1-2 grams/kg PO/PR

blocks.text:
Epiglottitis &
Croup

1. Croup is a respiratory illness characterized by inspiratory stridor, barking cough, and
hoarseness.
a. These symptoms result from inflammation in the larynx and subglottic airway.
b. Although croup is usually mild and self-limiting, significant upper airway
obstruction and respiratory distress can occur
2. Epiglottitis refers to inflammation of the epiglottis and adjacent supraglottic structures,
primarily due to infection. Without treatment, epiglottitis can progress to life-threatening
airway obstruction.
a. Abrupt onset and rapid progression (within hours) of upper airway obstruction are
hallmarks of bacterial epiglottitis
b. Patients with epiglottitis and impending complete airway obstruction may also
assume the "tripod" posture, a sitting position with the trunk leaning forward,
neck hyperextended, and chin thrust forward in an effort to maximize the
diameter of the obstructed airway

ADULT:

o Numbness or weakness of the face, arm, or leg, especially on one side of the
body
o Confusion, trouble speaking, or understanding
o Trouble seeing in one or both eyes
o Trouble walking, dizziness, loss of balance, or coordination
o Severe headache with no known cause
• Ensure adequate oxygenation and ventilation.
o Unless there are signs of respiratory distress, apply oxygen only if SpO2 is < 94%
• Check blood glucose and treat as needed per Altered Mental Status

• Any potential stroke patient should be NPO

o If the initial stroke screen is positive, the patient should be considered to have a
stroke.

HERE

o Oregon: BEFAST

o Hawaii: C-STAT
o Idaho: No state specific scale, though VAN is recommended
o Montana: VAN
• Transport patient in supine position with no head elevation.
o If the patient is unable to tolerate lying flat, provide minimal head elevation
• Document serial neurological examinations q 15 minutes
• See PEARLS for destination decision making

1. General time windows for intervention; these may vary depending on receiving facility
a. IV thrombolytics – 4.5 hours from LKW (facility arrival and entry by 4 hours)
b. Endovascular thrombectomy – 24 hours from LKW (facility arrival by 22 hours)
2. Stroke Destination Decisions for Stroke Screen Positive patients are based on:
a. Stroke Severity (LVO screen positive or negative)
b. Time LKW
c. State destination procedures (Washington)
d. Transport time
3. Idaho / Oregon / Montana / Hawaii Stroke Transport Guidelines (WA is #4 below)
a. VAN, BEFAST or C-STAT Positive
i. Preference is to transport to closest Comprehensive Stroke Center (CSC)
with endovascular capability.
ii. If patient is < 4 hours from LKW:
• Transfer to CSC if able to arrive within 4-hour window.
• If arrival (and entry through doors) at CSC will be after 4 hours since
LKW, but arrival at a closer primary or stroke capable hospital can
be made < 4-hour time since LKW:   Go to the closest hospital to
allow consideration of thrombolytics.
iii. If patient is >4 hours since LKW:
• These patients may benefit from endovascular therapy up to 24 hr
after last known well LKW.
• Transport per local EMS protocols or direction of OLMC, or transport
to closest thrombectomy-capable stroke center if:
• Patient is stable AND
• Transport time is no more than 2 hours greater than closest stroke-
ready facility AND
• Arrival to endovascular facility will be ≤22 hours from LKW, allowing
time for evaluation and procedure under 24 hours)
iv. If patient is >22 hours since LKW- transport to closest stroke ready facility

Determine Last Known Well (LKW) time
Conduct Stroke Screen according to state EMS requirements1,2,3,4
If the initial stroke screen is positive, the patient should be considered to have a stroke.
Perform a stroke severity screen (LVO screen)

HERE

VAN, BEFAST or C-STAT Positive
Preference is to transport to closest Comprehensive Stroke Center (CSC) with endovascular capability.
If patient is < 4 hours from LKW:
Transfer to CSC if able to arrive within 4-hour window.

If arrival (and entry through doors) at CSC will be after 4 hours since LKW, but arrival at a closer primary or stroke capable hospital can be made < 4-hour time since LKW: Go to the closest hospital to allow consideration of thrombolytics.
If patient is >4 hours since LKW:
These patients may benefit from endovascular therapy up to 24 hr after last known well LKW.
Transport per local EMS protocols or direction of OLMC, or transport
to closest thrombectomy-capable stroke center if
Patient is stable AND
Transport time is no more than 2 hours greater than closest stroke- ready facility AND
Arrival to endovascular facility will be ≤22 hours from LKW, allowing time for evaluation and procedure under 24 hours)
If patient is >22 hours since LKW- transport to closest stroke ready facility

Patients on DOACs (or other contraindication for thrombolytics) may also benefit bypass of primary stroke center.

1. Apply supplemental oxygen to maintain SpO2 ≥ 94%.
2. Place the mother supine with knees bent and widely separated.
a. Elevate the patient’s buttocks if needed.
3. Carefully assist expulsion of the newborn from the birth canal in its natural progression.
a. Provide gentle pressure using your palm to control delivery of the head. Do not
pull the newborn.
4. As the head emerges, encourage the mother not to push so that the delivery process can
continue slowly and with minimal trauma to the perineal area.
5. Gently guide the head downward (posterior) until the upper (anterior) shoulder delivers.
6. If the cord is wrapped around the newborn’s neck, attempt to unwrap it from the neck.
a. If unable, attach 2 umbilical clamps and cut the cord between the clamps.
7. Gently lift the head upwards (anterior) until the lower (posterior) shoulder delivers.
8. After delivery, assess infant per newborn management & resuscitation protocol.
9. Assess infant using APGAR at time of birth and five minutes later
a. Do not delay resuscitation to obtain APGAR.
10. Documentation should describe the infant using criteria rather than giving a numerical
score.
11. If no resuscitation is needed (term infant, breathing or crying, good muscle tone),
proceed as below.
12. Do not suction infant’s nose and mouth unless unable to maintain a patent airway.
13. At 1 to 3 minutes after delivery, clamp and cut the umbilical cord about 6 inches from
infant.
14. If resuscitation is needed, cord may be clamped and cut as soon as necessary.
15. Briefly dry infant and place on mother’s chest, in skin-to-skin contact.
a. Cover both with a clean, dry blanket.
16. Do not delay transport to deliver the placenta.
a. After the placenta has delivered, gently externally massage uterus to encourage
contraction and prevent bleeding.
17. If mother has significant postpartum hemorrhage (> 500 mL), continue uterine massage,
treat for shock, and update receiving facility.
18. Unless infant needs treatment, keep on mother’s chest for transport. Monitor vital signs
of mother and infant during transport.

a. With a gloved hand, GENTLY but firmly attempt to push the baby up the vagina

1. The presentation of an arm or leg through the vagina is an indication for immediate

2. Assess for presence of pulse in umbilical cord if prolapsed

Breech Presentation (continued)
6. After spontaneous delivery to the umbilicus, disengage the legs if they have not delivered
spontaneously. Pinard maneuver.
a. Abduct the hip by pushing laterally on the inner aspect of the knee.
b. Flex the knee and sweep the foot and leg medially, maneuvering it downward to
deliver.
c. Repeat for the delivery of opposite leg.
7. Rotate trunk to the anterior/posterior diameter for passage through the ischial spine. Allow
further descent to the scapula to occur spontaneously while supporting the body.
8. Arms can usually be delivered by hooking index finger over the baby’s shoulder, following the
humerus, and sweeping first one and then the other arm across the fetal chest and out over
the perineum.
9. After shoulders delivered, rotate baby’s trunk so back is anterior.
10. Apply gently downward traction until hairline is visible.
11. Rest chest and abdomen on palm of hand and forearm with the index and middle fingers
supporting the chin and fetal maxilla. With your other hand, support back and shoulders,
hooking two fingers over the shoulders and applying gently traction.
12. Bring baby gently upward while the second crew member applies suprapubic pressure to
facilitate delivery of the head.
13. Actions should be slow/controlled to allow chin, face, and brow to sweep over perineum.
14. Clear away with bulb syringe.
15. Ensure fetal airway. Clamp cord several inches from the infant’s navel using two sterile cord
clamps separated by two inches. Cut the cord between the clamps.
16. Wait for placenta to deliver spontaneously (up to 30min). For retained placenta:
a. If there is minimal bleeding, no aggressive attempt to remove the placenta is required
prior to transport.
b. If significant bleeding is present, consult with the receiving physician.
c. Never pull on the umbilical cord to deliver placenta.
17. When the placenta is delivered, place it in a bag and take it to the hospital for inspection.
18. Perform fundal massage following deliver of the placenta until the uterus is firm. Check for
fundal height and firmness q15 min for the initial hour following delivery.
19. In the event of post-partum hemorrhage, see Post-Partum Hemorrhage
Shoulder Dystocia:3
1. Once shoulder dystocia is suspected, forcible rotation or traction on the head should NOT be
attempted. A set of planned maneuvers must be executed in an attempt to atraumatically
deliver the shoulder using maternal expulsive efforts.
2. The initial maneuver is McRoberts whereby the maternal hips and legs are flexed until thighs
touch the maternal abdomen.
a. Downward suprapubic pressure is applied by an assistant followed by gentle
downward traction on the infant with maternal pushing.
b. Do NOT pull on the infant’s head and overstretch the neck.
3. If the McRoberts maneuver does not elicit delivery, additional maneuvers include:
a. Rotation of the anterior shoulder forward or backward out of the AP diameter of the
pelvis.
b. Delivery of the posterior arm by sweeping it across the fetal chest and over the
perineum.
c. See Vertex Delivery (below) and neonatal resuscitation for post-delivery
management.

Complications

Vertex Delivery:4
1. Position patient to allow maximum visualization and decrease fetal compromise. If
currently transporting via helicopter, consider asking the pilot to land if additional access
is required.
2. Encourage patient to “pant” to avoid pushing while setting up clean area for delivery.
3. Provide supplemental maternal oxygen.
4. Support perineum with hand or towel to decrease risk of perineum tearing.
5. Gently wipe mucous from baby’s mouth and nose as head clears perineum.
a. Check for nuchal cord and reduce as needed. See Nuchal/Prolapsed Cord above.
6. Allow rotation to occur without interference.
7. Support and allow the anterior shoulder to present first. Assist, if necessary, with a
downward motion.
a. After delivery of the anterior shoulder, if necessary, assist deliver of the posterior
shoulder with an upward motion
8. Support trunk as it delivers.
9. Ensure fetal airway. Suction if obvious obstruction due to secretions or if likely to need
positive- pressure ventilation. The mouth is suctioned first and then the nares to
decrease the risk for aspiration.
10. Treat newborn per Newborn Management.
11. Clamping the umbilical cord may be delayed for at least 30 – 60 seconds after birth in
vigorous term and preterm infants.
12. Place baby skin-to-skin with mother during delay.
13. Clamp cord several inches from the infant’s navel using sterile cord clamps, separated
by two inches.
a. Cut cord between clamps.

1. Nuchal cord describes an umbilical cord that passes 360 degrees around the fetal neck.
2. Breech presentation, which occurs in approximately 3 percent of fetuses at term, describes
the fetus whose presenting part is the buttocks and/or feet.
a. Frank breech – Both hips are flexed and both knees are extended so that the feet are
adjacent to the head (figure 1); accounts for 50 to 70 percent of breech fetuses at
term.
b. Complete breech – Both hips and both knees are flexed (figure 2); accounts for 5 to 10
percent of breech fetuses at term.
c. Incomplete breech presentation - One or both hips are not completely flexed (figure
3); accounts for 10 to 40 percent of breech fetuses at term.
3. Shoulder dystocia  is diagnosed when, after delivery of the fetal head, further expulsion of
the infant is prevented by impaction of the fetal shoulders within the maternal pelvis.
a. It is an obstetric emergency; thus, the obstetric provider must be able to recognize a
shoulder dystocia immediately and proceed through an orderly sequence of steps to
accomplish delivery in a timely manner.
b. The goal is to prevent fetal asphyxia, permanent Erb's palsy, or death, while also
avoiding physical injury (e.g., fetal fracture, maternal tissue trauma), but the latter is
acceptable if needed to prevent permanent injury of the child.
4. Vertex presentations is when the head of the fetus most commonly faces to the right and
slightly to the rear.
a. This position is said to be the most usual one because the fetus is thus best
accommodated to the shape of the uterus.
5. Uterine inversion occurs when the uterine fundus collapses into the endometrial cavity,
turning the uterus partially or completely inside out.
a. Although a rare complication of vaginal or cesarean birth, it is a life-threatening
obstetric emergency because, if not promptly recognized and treated, uterine
inversion can lead to severe hemorrhage and shock, resulting in maternal death.

Breech Presentation:2

If the head is not delivered within 3 minutes, suffocation can occur

Assess for presence of pulse in umbilical cord, if presenting

& PIH

• Seizure Management:
o Should seizure activity occur or persist; magnesium sulfate is the drug of choice
for treatment and to prevent reoccurrence:
▪ Administer an additional bolus of Magnesium Sulfate 2 grams over 2
minutes
▪ Increase magnesium sulfate infusion by 1 gram/hr
o If seizure persists more than 2 minutes, consider administer a benzodiazepine
(see seizure guideline) to control seizure while infusing magnesium sulfate
o Confirm patient is in a lateral position and protected from injury
o Administer oxygen by NRB or BVM. Establish an airway as needed
o Protect the patient from harm but do not restrain
• BP management:
o The goal SBP is 140 – 150 AND DBP is 90 – 100
▪ Treat until both the systolic and diastolic BP thresholds are met
o Uncontrolled decrease in BP or overcorrection may cause inadequate
uteroplacental perfusion and fetal distress
o If BP requires treatment, administer one of the following:
▪ Labetalol 20 mg IV over 2 minutes
• If BP thresholds are still exceeded after 10 min, administer 40 mg IV
over 2 minutes
• If BP thresholds are still exceeded after an additional 10 min,
administer 80 mg IV over 2 minutes
• If BP is still not controlled, consider Labetalol infusion at 1 – 2
mg/min (max of 300 mg in 24 hours), OR
▪ Hydralazine 5 mg IV over 1 minute
• If BP thresholds are still exceeded after 10 min, administer 5 – 10
mg IV every 20 minutes to a maximum cumulative dosage of 20 mg
• Consider a hydralazine infusion at 0.5 – 10 mg/hr

blocks.text:
1. Pre-Eclampsia: Triad of hypertension, proteinuria and edema developing at or beyond 20
weeks gestation, although edema is no longer required for the diagnosis
a. Mild preeclampsia is the presence of a BP >140/90 and >300 mg proteinuria in 24
hours
b. Severe preeclampsia is defined by the presence of any of the following:
i. SBP>160 or DBP>110 recorded on 2 occasions, 6 hours apart
ii. Proteinuria of >5 grams/24 hours
iii. Oliguria (< 400 mL/24 hours or < 30 mL/hour for 2+ hours)
iv. Visual disturbances
v. Epigastric pain, nausea vomiting
vi. Pulmonary edema
vii. HELLP syndrome (hemolysis, elevated live function and low platelets).
viii. Fetal growth restriction
2. Eclampsia: seizures in pregnancy not related to another cause
3. Chronic hypertension: hypertension before pregnancy or developing prior to the 20th
week of pregnancy; women with chronic hypertension may develop superimposed
preeclampsia

• Maternal resuscitation is the highest priority
• Assess vital signs
• Determine mechanism of injury and use of restraint devices.
• Inspect the abdomen for signs of contractions, contusion, abrasion, ecchymosis, or
other signs of trauma.
• Distinguish abdominal pain from contractions. Placental abruption often presents as a
rigid, painful abdomen. Vaginal bleeding may or may not be present. See Vaginal
Bleeding.
• Assess for potential chest injury. This is important because the mother’s elevated
diaphragm in pregnancy increases the risk of atelectasis leading to hypoventilation. Any
hypoxia will lead to shunting of blood from uterus.
• Perform serial assessments of abdomen and perineum along with notation of amount
and color of vaginal bleeding.
o If interfacility, the sending facility should perform a pelvic examination, when
possible, to determine cervical dilation and effacement as part of the assessment
for preterm labor that may develop following trauma.
o See Preterm Labor & Premature Rupture of Membranes.
• When transferring a patient from another facility, review fetal monitor strip, obtain report
and a copy if available.
o Specifically note any late or variable decelerations. 8. Initial treatment for
hypotension is to place the patient in a left lateral tilt position by inserting a wedge
under the right hip or tipping the backboard if immobilized.

blocks.text:
1. Abruptio Placentae:
a. Premature separation of the placenta after the 20th week of gestation and prior
to birth.
b. This is a clinical diagnosis based on findings of abdominal/back pain, uterine
tenderness, uterine contractions, and fetal distress.
c. Placental abruption may or may not result in vaginal bleeding.
2. Placenta Previa:
a. The classic presentation is painless vaginal bleeding, usually in the second or
third trimester. Uterine contractions may or may not be present.
b. The uterus is soft and pain free and fetal distress is usually not present.
Coagulopathy is less common with previa.

o If bleeding is uncontrolled, elevate limb and use direct pressure to site or pressure
points. Apply a bulky pressure dressing after you have controlled bleeding.
Continue to apply direct pressure to site or pressure points

proximal to the injury, directly over exposed skin. Record the time tourniquet was
applied. Do not loosen or remove tourniquet without an order from a physician

dressing

splint is applied

wound, then splint
• If appropriate and time permits, apply traction splint for suspected mid shaft or proximal
femur fracture.

traction is minimal or just enough to hold the limb at normal length

• For amputations, do the following to prepare the part for transport:
o Clean gross debris from amputated part

General Trauma
Care
CONTINUES TO NEXT PAGE

• Abdomen
o Assess for contusions, wounds, or eviscerated tissues
o Gently palpate to assess tenderness, rigidity, guarding
o Cover open wounds with dry sterile dressing
o Cover any eviscerated organs with sterile moist saline dressing
• Pelvis/GU
o Assess for instability (unless previous instability reported), swelling,
discoloration, bleeding, or blood at urethral meatus, if possible
o Compress iliac crests only once (from the side) to evaluate for pain/instability
▪ Do not distract (push down) as it increases bleeding space
▪ Do not repeatedly or vigorously manipulate the pelvis in patients with
fractures, as clots can become dislodged and increase blood loss.
o Apply pelvic binder for pelvic instability or pain
o Control bleeding by direct pressure
o Consider urinary catheter for interfacility trauma transports if there is no blood at
the urethral meatus
• Extremities
o Assess for bleeding, contusions, deformities, and swelling.
o Assess neurovascular status of all extremities by noting presence of pulses, skin
color and gross motor and sensory function.
o Control bleeding by direct pressure and cover all open wounds with dry sterile
dressings.
• Neurologic
o Assess mental status and note GCS.
o Assess gross motor and sensory function.
o See Head Injuries
• Continually reassess patient for changes or new findings
o Monitor and document response to all interventions
• Perform and document serial neurologic, cardiac, respiratory, and abdominal exams if
applicable
• Patients should be transported per state-specific trauma triage guidelines
o See Destination Determination
• Ensure Oregon trauma patients have a trauma band prior to arrival at accepting facility

blocks.text:
ADULT and PEDIATRIC:
1. Signs of increased intracranial pressure/herniation:
a. In patients with an initial GCS ≤ 8, a decrease in the GCS of more than two points.
b. A unilateral, dilated pupil is the hallmark sign of herniation. Progresses to bilateral and
fixed as herniation worsens
c. Decerebrate/extensor posturing
d. Cushing reflex (hypertension, bradycardia, irregular respirations/apnea)
e. Hemiparesis on side opposite the dilated pupil
2. The ETCO2 goal for all patients with known or suspected head injuries, including those with
suspected herniation is 35 – 40 mmHg.
a. Hyperventilation to obtain lower ETCO2 goals has not been shown to improve patient
outcomes.
3. Goal serum sodium is 144 – 155 mEq/L. If serum sodium is known and is ≥ 155 mEq/L, avoid
repeat hypertonic saline infusion unless all other options have failed to control herniation

not hemorrhage.

blocks.text:
ADULT and PEDIATRIC:
1. Pathophysiology:
a. Pooling of blood in lower extremities causes a decrease in the amount of blood
circulating to the vital organs
b. Factors worsening suspension trauma include inability to move legs, fatigue,
associated injuries, dehydration, hypothermia, and underlying cardiopulmonary
disease
c. Suspension trauma by itself or subsequent reperfusion of the lower extremities
may lead to loss of consciousness, renal failure, pulmonary embolus, or cardiac
arrest
2. Theories as to cause of death:
a. Blood pooled in the legs lacks oxygen and upon returning to the heart causes
ischemic heart failure
b. On horizontal positioning, a large volume of blood returns to the heart and
overloads the right ventricle
c. Reperfusion injury of the vital organs that became hypoxic during vertical
immobility
d. Injury caused by toxins that accumulated in the blood stored in the legs (similar to
crush injury)
3. Recognize some authorities suggest positioning patient in a sitting position for at least 30
min before horizontal positioning in order to prevent reperfusion injuries. Others
recommend immediate supine positioning, particularly when there are other injuries.
There is no consensus opinion regarding this issue.
a. You may encounter resistance from EMS first responders or bystanders when
attempting to immobilize or treat the patient in a supine position.

ADULTS and PEDIATRIC:
1. Pregnancy: Patients in the second half of pregnancy (uterine fundus above the umbilicus) should
be resuscitated with constant manual uterine displacement to minimize uterocaval
compression.
a. Alternatively, maintain left lateral tilt position of at least 15 degrees
2. The 'medical' arrest in the trauma setting: Patients without obvious major injury or those involved
in low energy mechanisms should be suspected of having had a primary cardiac arrest prior to
injury.
a. In such situations it would be appropriate to follow standard resuscitation algorithms
3. A substantial portion of traumatic arrests are caused by tension pneumothorax. If there is
suspected trauma (blunt or penetrating) to the trunk of the patient.
a. Unless the possibility of tension pneumothorax can be reliably and rapidly excluded,
bilateral decompression should be performed - with clinician discretion as to whether
rapid needle decompression is performed prior to finger thoracostomy while preparing for
the more invasive procedure.
4. The absence of obvious chest injuries should not be used to “entirely exclude” chest trauma.
a. Examples that you MAY be able to exclude chest trauma include GSW to the head,
exsanguination from amputations, etc…
b. When in doubt, decompress!
5. Trauma arrest with asystole is not survivable.

6. Trauma patients without pulses but with continued cardiac activity have a beating heart which is
not effectively pumping. They are LOST (Low Output State in Trauma).
a. Once you have completed chest decompression, airway securement, and blood/fluid
resuscitation, consider the use of epinephrine (push dose/infusion) to help maintain
baseline perfusion.
7. Baseline perfusion does not equate to a measurable blood pressure, but rather a slight increase
in ETCO2, a change in skin color, or other findings that do not directly result in a strong palpable
pulse in the hypovolemic patient.

Consider supraglottic airway or crash airway
Perform bilateral needle thoracostomies, unless chest trauma is entirely excluded per mechanism, history, and physical exam

The treatment of underlying causes of traumatic arrest should be prioritized over the administration of epinephrine and other ACLS medications

Pregnancy: Patients in the second half of pregnancy (uterine fundus above the umbilicus) should be resuscitated with constant manual uterine displacement to minimize uterocaval compression.
Alternatively, maintain left lateral tilt position of at least 15 degrees

The 'medical' arrest in the trauma setting: Patients without obvious major injury or those involved in low energy mechanisms should be suspected of having had a primary cardiac arrest prior to injury.
In such situations it would be appropriate to follow standard resuscitation algorithms
A substantial portion of traumatic arrests are caused by tension pneumothorax. If there is suspected trauma (blunt or penetrating) to the trunk of the patient.

Unless the possibility of tension pneumothorax can be reliably and rapidly excluded, bilateral decompression should be performed - with clinician discretion as to whether rapid needle decompression is performed prior to finger thoracostomy while preparing for the more invasive procedure.
The absence of obvious chest injuries should not be used to “entirely exclude” chest trauma.
Examples that you MAY be able to exclude chest trauma include GSW to the head, exsanguination from amputations, etc…
When in doubt, decompress!
Trauma arrest with asystole is not survivable.
Trauma patients without pulses but with continued cardiac activity have a beating heart which is not effectively pumping. They are LOST (Low Output State in Trauma).
Once you have completed chest decompression, airway securement, and blood/fluid resuscitation, consider the use of epinephrine (push dose/infusion) to help maintain baseline perfusion.

Baseline perfusion does not equate to a measurable blood pressure, but rather a slight increase in ETCO2, a change in skin color, or other findings that do not directly result in a strong palpable pulse in the hypovolemic patient.
