4. Administration Notes:
o Use a blood warming device for blood product administration, when possible. If
the patient requires an infusion rate that is higher than the warming device can
provide, you should weigh the risk vs
o benefit of rapid transfusion vs cold blood.
o Plasma and RBCs may be given sequentially, but not simultaneously, via the same
IV set. If multiple lines are available, you may administer them simultaneously.
o Connect blood tubing directly to an 18ga or larger IV catheter.
▪ For pediatric patients, connect to the largest available catheter (minimum
22ga).
▪ It is acceptable to use an intraosseous line in adult and pediatric patients if
no IV is available.
o Take pre-transfusion temperature and re-check temperature 15 min after initiation
of the transfusion. Repeat this for each unit transfused.
o Monitor for signs of potential transfusion reactions including fever (T>38°C or an
increase of 1°C above starting temperature).
5. Blood products received from sending facilities for transport:
o Flight crew will ensure blood products are administered within 4 hours from
removal from blood bank. Flight crew will note time of release from blood bank on
blood transfer form supplied by
o sending facility.
o Flight crew will verify blood products to recipient via blood bank number, name
and date of birth. Crew will document on supplied blood bank transfer forms.
o Unused blood products may be transferred to receiving facility blood bank given
appropriate transfer forms are in place.
▪ Alternatively, blood may be returned to the sending facility if local to the
home base.
▪ Any partially administered units or discontinued units will be discarded in a
biohazard bag and left with receiving facility blood bank
6. TXA may be given concurrently with blood products but must be given though a separate
line.
o Upon transfer of care at the receiving facility, the accepting physician and nurse
must be advised that no TXA infusion was initiated due to the total dose being
given via a one-time bolus.
o You may encounter patients with a TXA infusion that was started prior to your
arrival. That infusion should be continued and is generally given over 8 hours.
7. Blood bank guidance is against the use of LR in same line as blood. However, LR is safe to
utilize and may be necessary when no other fluids are available or working with one IV
access. Avoid LR with blood to avoid questions, but don’t hesitate to utilize for patient
care when necessary.
8. Assumes no known or suspected head injuries, if present:
o Adults: SBP of 110
o Pediatric (age < 10 years): 90 + (age x2)

It is acceptable to use an intraosseous line in adult and pediatric patients if no IV is available.
Take pre-transfusion temperature and re-check temperature 15 min after initiation of the transfusion. Repeat this for each unit transfused.
Monitor for signs of potential transfusion reactions including fever (T>38°C or an increase of 1°C above starting temperature).
Blood products received from sending facilities for transport:
Flight crew will ensure blood products are administered within 4 hours from removal from blood bank. Flight crew will note time of release from blood bank on blood transfer form supplied by
sending facility.
Flight crew will verify blood products to recipient via blood bank number, name and date of birth. Crew will document on supplied blood bank transfer forms.
Unused blood products may be transferred to receiving facility blood bank given appropriate transfer forms are in place.
Alternatively, blood may be returned to the sending facility if local to the home base.
Any partially administered units or discontinued units will be discarded in a biohazard bag and left with receiving facility blood bank
TXA may be given concurrently with blood products but must be given though a separate
line.
Upon transfer of care at the receiving facility, the accepting physician and nurse must be advised that no TXA infusion was initiated due to the total dose being given via a one-time bolus.
You may encounter patients with a TXA infusion that was started prior to your arrival. That infusion should be continued and is generally given over 8 hours.

Blood bank guidance is against the use of LR in same line as blood. However, LR is safe to utilize and may be necessary when no other fluids are available or working with one IV access. Avoid LR with blood to avoid questions, but don’t hesitate to utilize for patient care when necessary.
Assumes no known or suspected head injuries, if present:
Adults: SBP of 110
Pediatric (age < 10 years): 90 + (age x2)
PEDIATRIC
For children < 12 yo or any patient < 50 kg, acceptable plasma is limited to Group AB liquid plasma, thawed Group AB FFP, or Low Titer Group A Liquid Plasma (LTGAP)
DO NOT use Group A liquid plasma or thawed Group A FFP with this patient population

9. Drape area using sterile towels
10. The incision site is lateral to the nipple (4th or 5th intercostal space) between the anterior
and mid-axillary lines
11. Using a #10 scalpel, make a 2” transverse incision between the anterior and mid-axillary
lines, lateral to the nipple or inframammary crease
a. Cut directly over the 5th or 6th rib, but not to the rib
12. Using a large Kelly clamp and holding the instrument by the shanks, push the tip through
the soft tissue until touching the rib
13. Carefully press the Kelly clamp over the top of the rib and through the intercostal
muscles to enter the pleural space
b. Avoid the inferior rib border as vessels and nerves run though this area
14. Enlarge the pleural opening by spreading the Kelly clamp as you pull it from the pleural
space
15. Insert a gloved finger through the opening to verify you have entered the pleura
c. Most easily done by “hooking” your finger to touch the inner side of the ribs
d. Keep in mind that rib fractures may be present and can cause lacerations
16. Insert the chest tube using the large Kelly clamp. Direct the tube cephalad and posterior
until all the holes are inside the chest
e. Note tube depth marking which should be >6cm
17. Attach the Heimlich valve and evaluate the patency of the tube
f. Fluctuation of the valve with ventilation and improvement in compliance or
respiratory status are indications of proper placement and patency
18. Secure the chest tube with towel clamps, quick ties, and tape
19. Tape the chest tube and Heimlich valve to the thorax. Tape any connections as needed.
The Heimlich valve may be connected to low suction
20. If the chest tube output is >1000mL blood in less than 60 minutes, clamp the tube to
avoid exsanguination
g. This will cause hemothorax with thought to tamponade further bleeding. Monitor
for signs/symptoms of a recurrent tension pneumothorax
h. Notify receiving of output and clamped tube as patient likely to need emergent OR
21. Document the name of the receiving physician who verified proper placement of the
chest tube before finalizing clinical chart
i. Do not document the procedure was “successful” without documenting the name
of the physician who verified placement
j. If the crew is told their placement was incorrect, immediately notify the Clinical
Manager on Call and complete a QM report

b. If the defibrillator is not discharged within 60 seconds

blocks.text:
1. Identify you have second defibrillator that can be used to utilize Dual Sequential External
Defibrillation (DSED)
2. With minimal CPR interruption, place a second set of pads, ensuring there is no overlap
or contact with the other set
a. If there is overlap of pads there is a significant risk of damaging the defibrillators.
If the first set is placed anterior lateral position, place the second set in anterior
posterior fashion and vice versa
3. One provider will be operating both defibrillators to ensure the administration of the
shocks are as close together as possible but not at the same time, ideally less than one
second apart.
4. While chest compressions are occurring, charge both defibrillators to the maximum
setting and once these have charged, stop CPR for a pulse and rhythm check. Confirm
refractory V-Fib/V-Tach is present on both monitors.
5. If confirmed, press the shock button on the first monitor stating “shock one” when
delivered and then immediately press the shock button on the second monitor stating
“shock two”
6. Resume CPR.
7. Repeat every two minutes until ROSC is achieved or termination of refractory V-Fib/V-
Tach.

Preparation for Transport:
1. Gather equipment and the sending provider to help if needed
2. Verify the dose that is being given with the sending provider, and it is being dosed in IBW.
a. Typical doses are 10-50 nanograms/kg/minute
b. Ensure you have enough epoprostenol for the transport, if not request additional
medication.
3. Ask the sending provider to familiarize you with the functions of the syringe pump and
troubleshooting any issues or alarms that may arise.
4. Ensure the T-1 checks have been completed, and the ventilator tubing is ready to switch over.
5. Place two filters on the expiratory limb and one filter on the inspiratory limb closest to the
Hamilton.
6. Switch the patient to LFN T-1 Hamilton ventilator and place the epoprostenol that is infusing
via the Aerogen on the inspiratory limb after the filter.
7. Unplug the Aerogen controller just prior to leaving the bedside and bring this with you.
a. If you are using the USB version plug this directly into the Hamilton.
b. If you are using the Pro-X, once you unplug this it will revert to the 30-minute mode
while it is unplugged from AC power.
i. Once you are in the ambulance or the aircraft, plug the Pro-X back into the
wall and confirm AC power.
ii. This is a good time to plug in your syringe pump and Hamilton as well.

Ensure you have enough epoprostenol for the transport, if not request additional medication.
Ask the sending provider to familiarize you with the functions of the syringe pump and troubleshooting any issues or alarms that may arise.
Ensure the T-1 checks have been completed, and the ventilator tubing is ready to switch over.
Place two filters on the expiratory limb and one filter on the inspiratory limb closest to the Hamilton.
Switch the patient to LFN T-1 Hamilton ventilator and place the epoprostenol that is infusing via the Aerogen on the inspiratory limb after the filter.
Unplug the Aerogen controller just prior to leaving the bedside and bring this with you.
If you are using the USB version plug this directly into the Hamilton.
If you are using the Pro-X, once you unplug this it will revert to the 30-minute mode while it is unplugged from AC power.
Once you are in the ambulance or the aircraft, plug the Pro-X back into the wall and confirm AC power.
This is a good time to plug in your syringe pump and Hamilton as well.
During Transport
Ensure the Aerogen solo cup remains upright and the syringe pump is free of alarms.
Monitor the PA pressures if there is a PA catheter present.
Report any changes to the receiving facility.
Ensure the receiving hospital has report so they can gather necessary equipment and have it ready.
We do not titrate this medication without an order from a physician.
After Transport
Ensure you gather all of the sending hospital’s equipment.
Contact the CM or BAM to get the equipment back to the sending.
If you are flying back over the sending, you can coordinate with the CMOC to drop if off at the hospital.
Epoprostenol has an extremely short half-life and cannot be stopped during transport.
The Aerogen solo cup must stay upright throughout the transport

Equipment:
• All equipment and medications required for intubation
• Bougie
Procedure:
1. Delineate roles for the procedure:
a. Operator will be the crew member performing the tube exchange.
b. Assistant will be the crew member assisting the operator with the exchange.
2. Initiate pre-oxygenation by increasing FiO2 to 100% and place a NC @ 15 LPM.
3. Additional sedation and paralytic agents should be administered.
a. See Rapid Sequence Induction (RSI)
4. Move the patient as needed to optimize operator position, lighting, and patient safety
5. Hold the ETT and have the assistant remove the device or tape securing the ETT
6. Have the assistant advance the bougie into the existing endotracheal tube and advance gently
until the markings that indicate the catheter is properly positioned mid trachea.
7. Stop advancement if hold up is encountered and avoid advancing the bougie deeper than mid-
trachea
8. The bougie must be maintained in this position for the duration of the procedure
9. Perform laryngoscopy with the video laryngoscope and identify the original tube with the bougie
inserted in the glottic opening
10. Asses the surrounding structure and anatomy for any abnormalities that may impede the
procedure.
11. Maintain the view of the glottic opening throughout the procedure until the new tube is in place
12. Deflate the cuff
13. While the assistant maintains control and position of the bougie, the operator carefully
withdraws the ETT under direct vision until the tip clears the mouth.
14. Once the ETT tip is clear, the operator takes and maintains control and position of the bougie.
15. The assistant carefully removes the ETT over the bougie.
16. The assistant loads the new ETT onto the bougie and carefully advances until the tip of the ETT
reaches the patients mouth and the bougie extends from the proximal end of the ETT.
17. The assistant takes and maintains control and position of the bougie exiting the ETT while the
operator takes and maintains control of the ETT and continues to advance it
18. While maintaining laryngoscopic view, the tube is advanced into the trachea over the bougie
using a 90-degree counter-clockwise to prevent its beveled point from getting caught in the
arytenoid cartilage
19. Inflate the ETT cuff, carefully remove the bougie, verify placement and secure the ETT..

ADULT & PEDIATRIC:
1. ETT exchange is an airway procedure, which risks injury or loss of airway
2. The ETT exchange procedure must always be performed with visualization of the glottic opening
and must NEVER be performed blind
3. To make ETT exchange safe we want to make this procedure as similar as possible to standard
intubation procedures
a. If we are following similar approaches compared to most intubations, when things go
sideways, we can apply the usual principles of airway management

1. Gather the appropriate advanced procedure kit from the airway bag
2. Cleanse the site with chlorhexidine/isopropanol swabs
3. Don a mask and eye protection, then sterile gloves
4. Make a sterile work area and assemble the instruments
5. The incision site is lateral to the nipple (4th or 5th intercostal space) between the anterior
and mid-axillary lines. Patient size hand placed in the axilla for quick assessment.
6. Using a #10 scalpel, make a 2” transverse incision between the anterior and mid-axillary
lines, lateral to the nipple. If in doubt, err another rib interspace more superior.
a. Cut directly over the 5th or 6th rib, but not to the rib.
7. Using a large Kelly clamp and holding the instrument by the shanks, push the tip through
the soft tissue until touching the rib
8. Carefully press the Kelly clamp over the top of the rib and through the intercostal
muscles to enter the pleural space
a. Avoid the inferior rib border as vessels and nerves run though this area
9. Enlarge the pleural opening by spreading the Kelly clamp as you pull it from the pleural
space
10. Insert a gloved finger through the opening to verify you have entered the pleura
a. Most easily done by “hooking” your finger to touch the inner side of the ribs
b. Keep in mind that rib fractures may be present and can cause lacerations
11. Consider placing a VENTED chest seal (Hyfin) or cover the site with a sterile gauze
12. In the event of excessive blood return (estimated>1000ml), place an occlusive dressing
over the site to prevent exsanguination and initiate blood product administration.
a. This will cause hemothorax with thought to tamponade further bleeding. Monitor
for signs/symptoms of a recurrent tension pneumothorax
b. Notify receiving of output and clamped tube as patient likely to need emergent OR
13. If the patient re-tensions, insert your finger into the existing incision

blocks.text:
Equipment:
• Flow-Safe II CPAP delivery system
• Oxygen source
• Appropriately sized mask
Procedure:
1. Explain the procedure to the patient
2. Select an appropriately sized mask for the patient
3. Determine the oxygen flow rate that corresponds to the desired PEEP level via the chart
attached to the oxygen tubing
4. Connect attached oxygen tubing to oxygen source
5. Set LPM flow to desired CPAP level
6. Gently hold the mask to the patient’s face while ensuring a good face/mask seal
7. Allow the patient to become comfortable with the mask and provide coaching, as
needed
8. Secure the Flow-Safe device to the patient via head straps
9. Check around the mask for any leaks and adjust mask and/or head strap accordingly via
the Velcro straps
a. Ensure that the white pads are seated flat on the forehead
10. Verify that the pressure indicated on the attached manometer corresponds with your
desired PEEP level
a. Note that the pressure indicated may be ± 3 cmH2O of your desired CPAP
b. Mask leaks will affect the desired CPAP level; attempt to reposition or change
mask size, if needed.
11. Titrate oxygen flow/PEEP level to patient’s oxygenation status
12. If nebulized medications are needed, connect nebulizer set up between the mask and
Flow-Safe manometer via T piece
13. Connect oxygen tubing for nebulizer to a secondary oxygen source
14. The mask can quickly be removed by unlatching the blue quick release clips at the
bottom of the mask

blocks.text:
Nasogastric tube: (preferred in awake patients)
1. Explain procedure to the patient
2. Measure the NG tube depth
a. End of the tube should be placed at the tip of the nose, extended to the corner of
the ear, and then to the xiphoid process
3. Lubricate the tube and insert it into one of the patient’s nares
a. Pass the tube gently along the floor of the nasal passage and advance as the
patient swallows
b. Remove the tube if the patient begins to cough or has new onset dyspnea
4. Assess for proper placement
a. Connect a 60mL syringe and aspirate back while assessing for gastric contents
b. Inject ~20 mL of air into the tube and listen/feel for an air rush in the stomach
5. Once placement is confirmed, secure tube in place with tape
a. Should NOT be taped to ETT
6. Place NG tube on suction as required

1. Measure the OG tube depth
a. End of the tube should be placed at corner of the mouth, extended to the tip of the
ear, and then to the xiphoid process

3. Assess for proper placement
a. Connect a 60mL syringe and aspirate back while assessing for gastric contents
b. Inject ~20 mL of air into the tube and listen/feel for an air rush in the stomach

blocks.text:
1. Open the package and remove gauze. Retain the packaging.
2. Remove any saturated gauze from the wound so that the hemostatic agent can directly
contact the bleeding vessels.
3. Pack rolled gauze into wound and use it to apply pressure directly on the bleeding
source.
4. Continue to apply direct pressure for 3 minutes.
5. If the dressing is fully red, then it must be removed and replaced with a new hemostatic
dressing.
a. The previous dressing may not have been applied directly to the bleeding source,
or adequate pressure may not have been held long enough.
6. Once bleeding is controlled, wrap, and tie the bandage to maintain pressure.
a. Attach the product packaging to the patient for transport with them to the
hospital.
7. Do not lift the dressing! “If you peek, you leak.”

effectively control “nuisance bleeding” such as head lacerations etc.
2. Dressings can remain in a wound for up to 24 hours.
3. QuickClot dressings are impregnated with an inorganic mineral agent Kaolin and do not
contain any human, animal, or shellfish product, or cause an exothermic reaction.

Procedure:
1. Ensure nasal passages are patent. Suction PRN
a. Utilize saline PRN for thick secretions
2. Keep patient NPO
3. Measure nares with size card and select appropriate RAM cannula
a. Prongs should not occlude > 80% of nares
4. Connect RAM cannula to ventilator circuit
5. Select “HiFloO2” mode under Noninvasive
6. Select desired FiO2 and flow rate
a. Titrate flow to work of breathing
b. Titrate FiO2 to oxygenation needs
7. If the patient deteriorates, consider CPAP, BiPAP, or intubation (RSI)
8. Utilize the LFN oxygen calculator to ensure you have enough oxygen to complete the
transport
Adult Flow Rates:
• 8 – 60 LPM
• Requires provider/OLMC approval for transport without heat/humidification
Pediatric Flow Rates:
• 0.5 – 1 L/kg/min
o May titrate up to 2 L/kg/min or 20 LPM if no heat/humidification

High Flow
Nasal Cannula

ADULT and PEDIATRIC:
1. High flow oxygen therapy delivers volumes of air over what the patient ventilates and
allows for the displacement of excess CO2 while increasing the amount of O2 delivered.
a. The therapeutic goal is to increase PaO2 thereby creating a grater oxygen diffusion
gradient, thus increasing overall oxygenation.
2. You may utilize regular oxygen tubing with a RAM cannula if the Hamilton T-1 isn’t readily
available to you.
a. Connects to typical flow meter “christmas tree.”
b. This method will result in a reduced max flow rate and lack of humidification.
3. High Flow Oxygen therapy can be used as a convenience option for hospitalized patients
as it allows them to eat and drink much easier. However, it may not be the best option for
transport.
a. Patients who require flows on the low end may be able to tolerate a NRB mask for
transport.
b. Patients with higher flow requirements may do better on CPAP or BiPAP during
transport.
4. Low Pressure Oxygen (LPO) mode is NOT available during HFNC therapy.
a. If LPO is needed to conserve oxygen, consider switching to CPAP or BiPAP
5. Guide to aid in understanding appropriate sizing of cannula (this does not supersede the
sizing card carried with the RAM Cannulas)

a. Loading and unloading the IABP from the aircraft at the referring and receiving facilities is
under the direction of LFN personnel
b. After loading IABP and patient in the rotor, secure the IABP between stretcher and aft-
facing seat
c. Using the foam pad under the pump (keeps pump off the brownline rail) and Pilatus tie-
down straps with metal buckles, run straps through the handle on the top of the pump

facing seat to the left of the patient loading door
e. Using the Pilatus tie-down straps with metal buckles, run straps through the handles on
the top of the pump
f. Ensure IABP is plugged into the aircraft power
2. Helium Use
a. The internal helium reservoir contains enough helium for 36 autofill cycles
b. Every time the pump is powered off or on and every time the balloon is
disconnected/reconnected, the pump performs 6 autofill cycles
c. The Maquet IABP contains a pressure transducer inside the helium gas shuttle circuit
d. This transducer senses changes in barometric pressure and gas
e. expansion/contraction, causing an automated “autofill” to occur as necessary to obtain
the correct balloon pressure. One autofill cycle will occur for every 1000 feet the aircraft
increases in altitude and for every 2000 feet of descent
f. There is an additional autofill cycle for every 2 hours of pump operation
3. Transferring from existing IABP to Maquet IABP
a. Turn on LFN Maquet IABP
b. Place ECG leads on patient, tape down connections and connect ECG cable to pump
c. Connect fiber-optic sensor cable first (if utilized)

i. NOTE: Even when using the fiber optic cable for timing, the pressure
cable/transducer should still be connected as a backup
ii. Elevate the NS flush bag at least 3 feet above patient from IAB transducer
iii. Ensure the pressure bag is inflated to 300 mmHg and flush the line for several
seconds, then press and hold the zero button for two seconds as noted on the
IABP screen
iv. NOTE: If patient has an Arrow fiber optic balloon, it will not “talk” to Maquet
console, and the pressure cable/transducer for the IAB must be used
v. Connect IAB helium tubing to console

EQUIPMENT:
• Appropriately sized i-gel©
• Lubricant
• ETCO2 adaptor
• Securement device
PROCEDURE:
1. Wearing gloves, open the cage pack and transfer the device to the lid of the cage
a. Place a small bolus of a water-based lubricant onto the smooth inner surface of
the cage
b. Do not use silicone-based lubricants
2. Grasp the i-gel© along the integral bite block and lubricate the back, sides, and front of
the cuff with a thin layer of lubricant
a. Ensure after lubrication has been completed that no bolus of lubricant remains in
the bowl of the cuff or elsewhere on the device
3. Grasp the lubricated i-gel© firmly along the integral bite block
a. Position the device so the i-gel© cuff outlet is facing towards the chin of the patient
4. The patient should be in the sniffing position with head extended and neck flexed unless
contraindicated due to trauma.
a. The chin should be gently pressed down before proceeding to insert the i-gel©
5. Introduce leading soft tip into the mouth of the patient in a direction towards the hard
palate
6. Glide the device downward and backward along the hard palate with a continuous but
gentle push until a definitive resistance is felt
7. Do not apply excessive force on the device during insertion
a. It is not necessary to insert fingers or thumbs into the patient’s mouth during the
process of inserting the device
8. If there is early resistance during insertion, perform a jaw thrust and insert the i-gel© with
a deep rotation

ADULT and PEDIATRIC:
1. Hamilton T1 Specific Information
• The fixed nebulizer flow, using 100% O2, is synchronized with the inspiratory phase of
each breath for 30 minutes.
• The built-in pneumatic nebulization feature is disabled:
o During neonatal ventilation
o When using HiFloO2 therapy
o When in LPO (low pressure oxygen) mode
• Connecting the nebulizer between the flow sensor and ETT will increase dead space
and may cause incorrect measurements.
• The oxygen consumption of a nebulizer attached to the device is not included in the
O2 consumption parameter value.
• If transporting a patient using an Aerogen nebulizer, connect the Aerogen to the
Hamilton T1 using the USB port found on the side of the ventilator.
• The ventilator provides a stable pressure source to power a pneumatic nebulizer
connected to the Nebulizer port, optimally specified for a flow of approximately 8
L/min.
• The ventilator automatically compensates the additional volume provided by the
pneumatic nebulizer to deliver the set tidal volume.
2. LTV  Specific Information
• The nebulization procedure can be performed on the ReVel ventilator using the build
in nebulization feature during volume breaths in Assist/Control mode only.
• When the nebulizer is activated, a six (6) L/min nominal flow is delivered to the
nebulizer drive port.
o This drives an aerosol nebulizer that doses medication into the patient circuit.
• The ventilator must be connected to a high-pressure oxygen source and a Nebulizer.
• The nebulizer flow is 100% oxygen, delivered to the Nebulizer port from the high
pressure O2 inlet.
• During nebulization, the ventilator decreases the flow to its inspiratory limb to
compensate for the addition of the nebulization flow at the patient Wye.

Indications
• Medication administration when IV access is
not present or is undesirable.
Contraindications
• Facial trauma
• Epistaxis
• Nasal congestion or discharge
• Recent nasal cocaine use
bullets: Medication administration when IV access is not present or is undesirable.

blocks.text:
Equipment:
1. Mucosal atomizer device (MAD)
2. Small volume syringe (1 – 3 mL)
3. Desired medication
Procedure:
1. Patient should be in a recumbent with head tilted back or supine.
2. Draw up medication into a 1 mL or 3 mL syringe.
a. An extra 0.1 mL of medication should be drawn into the syringe to account for
dead space within the atomizer
3. Expel any air within the syringe.
4. Attach the MAD firmly to the syringe.
5. Visually inspect nares and chose the largest nare or the one with the least obstruction.
6. Insert syringe with MAD attached into the nares until resistance is met (approximately 1.5
cm). Aim tip toward the top of the ipsilateral ear.
7. Timing the respirations, depress plunger rapidly upon patient exhalation but before
inhalation and deliver half of the total desired dose.
8. Repeat steps 6 and 7 in the opposite nare.
9. If the patient is sitting, compress the nares with a gloved finger for 1-2 min. after
administration.
10. The MAD is reusable on the same patient but must be disposed after each patient.
Considerations:
1. To improve success, minimize the drug volume and maximize concentration.
a. Ages ≥ 10 years: no more than 1 mL per nostril.
b. Pediatric (< 10 years of age): no more than 0.5 mL per nostril.
2. Medications that can be delivered IN include but are not limited to Fentanyl, Ketamine,
Midazolam, and Naloxone

Equipment:
• EZ-IO driver
• Appropriately sized IO needle
• EZ-IO securement kit
• 10 mL saline flush
• 2% lidocaine (if conscious)
Procedure:
1. Select an insertion site
a. Adult: proximal tibia, distal tibia, humeral head, and distal femur (only if ≤ 21 years)
b. Pediatric (> 3 kg): proximal tibia, distal tibia, humeral head, and distal femur
2. Determine the correct needle length
a. Palpate the intended insertion site with a finger to get a rough estimate of the depth
of tissue.
i. There is typically more tissue overlying the humeral head or femoral sites
than the proximal tibia. The distal tibia usually has the least amount of
overlying tissue
b. In general, the EZ-IO 45 mm (yellow hub) needle should be used for the humeral
site placement in patients weighing ≥ 40 kg
3. Prime the EZ-IO extension set with saline
4. If the patient is responsive to pain, consider providing pain management via 2% lidocaine
a. Refer to the flow chart below for steps
5. Prep insertion site with an antiseptic swab
a. Chlorhexidine, isopropyl alcohol, etc…
6. With the needle angled 90-degrees to the bone, push the needle tip though the skin until it
rests on the bone
a. The 5-mm mark, which is the most proximal mark to the hub must be visible above
the skin
i. If not, use a longer needle and/or insertion site to ensure adequate
placement depth
7. Gently squeeze trigger on driver and apply gentle, steady pressure
8. Immediately release trigger when you feel a sudden “pop” or loss of resistance
a. You have entered the medullary space
9. Disconnect driver from needle hub, remove stylet and place in the include sharps block or
in a sharps container
10. Place EZ-Stabilizer© dressing over the cannula hub
11. Attach primed EZ-Connect© extension set to hub
a. Secure by twisting clockwise and ensure clamp is open
12. Pull tabs from EZ-Stabilizer© to expose adhesive and adhere to skin

blocks.text:
Equipment:
• Transducer kit
• 1000 mL normal saline
• Pressure bag
• Cardiac monitor with applicable monitoring cable
Procedure:
1. Evaluate the invasive monitoring system to ensure it is functioning correctly and
accurately
a. If the current transducer is compatible with LFN equipment, you may use the
existing line
i. Continue to step #6
b. If the current transducer is NOT compatible with LFN equipment, you must switch
the line out
i. Continue to step #3
2. Remove air from IV fluid bag and then spike with the transducer tubing
3. Run fluid through tubing to prime and remove any existing air
a. Tap on locations where air may tend to accumulate
4. Clamp pressure tubing, place pressure bag on the fluids, and inflate bag to 300 mmHg
5. Replace all open stopcock caps with sterile dead-end caps and ensure connections are
tight
6. Connect transducer line to the cardiac monitor
7. Place and secure transducer at phlebostatic axis
8. Zero transducer line
a. Open stopcock to air
b. Observe for square waveform test
c. Press zero on cardiac monitor
d. Return stopcock to previous position and ensure the appropriate waveform
appears
e. Repeat this process with any change in altitude
9. Compare the difference in IBP and NIBP values

Invasive Hemodynamic
Monitoring

ADULT and PEDIATRIC:
1. If waveform is over dampened (flat waveform):
a. Check set up for air/kinks
b. Ensure pressure bag is appropriately inflated
c. Ensure no white caps are left in the set up
d. Ensure tubing is connected to the patient
e. Ensure transducer is properly positioned
f. Ensure waveform scale is correct
2. If the waveform is dampened:
a. Chest set up for air
b. Remove any extra tubing or stopcocks
3. For patients with a pulmonary artery catheter:
a. Do not infuse medications through the distal PA port
i. The right ventricular port should be used for medications. It may be
capped and flushed
b. Keep valve/stopcock open at all times
c. There is no indication for a PCWP pressure and thus should NOT be wedged.
i. Document PCWP prior to departure, if available
d. Ensure wedge balloon is deflated, locked in the OFF position, and the syringe
remains empty
i. If monitoring indicates a PCWP despite deflated balloon, contact medical
control for guidance

blocks.text:
Indications
• Unconscious patient with respiratory
compromise and an absent gag reflex
Contraindications
• Responsive patient with gag reflex
• Known esophageal disease
• Caustic ingestions
bullets: Unconscious patient with respiratory compromise and an absent gag reflex

blocks.text:
EQUIPMENT:
• King Airway and syringe of the appropriate size (see below)
• Airway securing device
• Suction
PROCEDURE:
1. Prepare suction and have it readily available
2. Select the correct size KING LT(S)-D based on the patient’s weight or height
3. Test the cuff inflation
4. Pre-oxygenate the patient
5. Position head in “sniffing” position or maintain spinal motion restriction, if indicated.
6. Hold the KING LT(S)-D with the dominant hand
7. Open the mouth and apply chin-lift with the non-dominant hand
8. Introduce the KING LT(S)-D into corner of mouth at 90° angle
9. As the tube tip passes under the tongue, rotate the tube back to midline
10. Insert the KING LT(S)-D until the flange of the connector aligns with the teeth. Do not
force insertion
11. Fully inflate the cuffs; the KING LT(S)-D will rise slightly as it seats
12. Do not discard the syringe; place it to the right of the patient’s head
13. Must attach ETCO2 to confirm placement and the BVM and ventilate while maintaining
gentle downward pressure
14. Assess for chest rise and fall, auscultate breath sounds bilaterally, and maintain
continuous ETCO2 monitoring. A normal four-phase waveform should be visible if
ventilating appropriately
15. If ventilation is not accomplished, without deflating the cuff, pull back slightly and re-
attempt ventilations. If pulling back slightly does not seat the device properly, then
deflate the cuff, slowly withdraw the tube and re-assess
16. Ventilate with oxygen at the appropriate rate (monitor for chest rise/fall, SpO2 and ETCO2)
17. If the KING LT(S)-D is removed, suction MUST be available.

blocks.text:
Adult and Pediatric:
• ETCO2 assessment must be performed and documented, for all advanced airway intubations
• Verify advanced airway placement with ETCO2
• Place patient on continuous capnography for the duration of transport
• In situations where there isn’t a consistent waveform, the ETT should be removed and ventilation
performed by other methods (BVM, SGA, or additional intubation attempt) OR perform direct
visualization of insertion of ETT through the vocal cords
• Consider insertion of an OG tube to decompress the stomach to facilitate ventilation
• Consider use of HMEF between the ETT/SGA and ETCO2 for secretions, blood or vomit, after
effective airway suctioning
• At times, operational aspects (secretions, blood, vomit) may interfere with effective ETCO2
measurement. If this situation occurs, there are (2) options:
o Remove the tube and provide effective BVM.
o Direct visualization of the location of the tube witnessed by another LFN or EMS provider.
▪ Utilize the recording feature of the CMAC.

Use and Placement
• Use an approved mechanical CPR device, such as LUCAS or ZOLL AutoPulse, based on
availability, patient fit, crew training, and transport setup.
• Follow manufacturer instructions, LFN training, and applicable clinical protocols for the selected
device.
• For LUCAS, place the back plate beneath the patient and align the suction cup/pressure pad over
the appropriate compression point.
• For ZOLL AutoPulse, position the patient on the platform, align the patient with device landmarks,
and close the LifeBand.
• Confirm device placement, patient alignment, and securement before movement whenever
feasible.
Prior to Transport
• Initiate immediate manual CPR.
• Apply defibrillation pads, AP position preferred
• Prepare the selected mechanical CPR device while manual CPR continues.
• Minimize CPR interruption during deployment (<10 seconds whenever possible).
• Confirm device-specific positioning before starting compressions.
• For AutoPulse, verify the LifeBand is not twisted and is free of obstruction. For LUCAS, verify the
suction cup/pressure pad is centered and the device is locked in place.
• Start the selected device and confirm effective compressions, including ETCO2 response when
available.

Device

During Transport
• The selected mechanical CPR device should remain active throughout movement and transport
unless clinically indicated or device troubleshooting requires a pause.
• Secure the patient and device to the stretcher or transport surface according to device and
transport requirements.
• Continue advanced cardiac life support per protocol.
• Defibrillation may be performed with the mechanical CPR device in place when pads are
appropriately positioned and safety precautions are followed.
• Monitor for device alarms, battery status, patient position, compression quality, and any device-
specific warnings.
• If the device malfunctions or cannot be safely used, immediately resume manual CPR.
Transport Considerations
• Secure all straps, tubing, device components, and power sources before movement, lift-off, or
departure.
• Follow vehicle, stretcher and equipment securing requirements.
• Monitor continuous use of ETCO2 to help verify adequate compression quality. In many
instances you may see higher than predicted ETCO2 values due to the compression quality.
• Recheck positioning of the CPR device after each move.
• Pulse and Rhythm Checks
• Pause only for rhythm analysis, pulse checks when indicated, defibrillation when indicated, or
airway procedures only when clinically necessary.
• Keep interruptions as brief as possible, with a maximum pause <10 seconds.
LUCAS Chest Compression System
• Continue high-quality manual CPR while preparing the device.
• Power on the LUCAS and allow the self-test to complete.
• During the next planned rhythm check, slide the back plate beneath the patient (below the
axillae) with the briefest possible interruption.
• Attach the upper frame to the back plate until both sides click securely.
• Position the suction cup over the lower half of the sternum, immediately above the xiphoid.
• Press the suction cup to the chest, select PAUSE to lock the start position, then begin
compressions (Continuous or 30:2 per protocol).
• Once the correct position is found for the suction cup, if possible use a marker to draw a circle
around the suction cup. This way if the LUCAS position moves you will notice it immediately.
• Apply the stabilization strap.
• Reassess device position after every patient movement or transfer and resume manual CPR
immediately if the device malfunctions.

blocks.text:
Mechanical CPR
Device

AutoPulse Mechanical CPR System
• Continue manual CPR while preparing the device.
• Power on the AutoPulse.
• During the next planned pause, transfer the patient onto the AutoPulse platform.
• Align the patient's axillae with the platform reference marks and ensure the torso is centered.
• Bring the LifeBand across the chest, ensuring it is flat (not twisted) and positioned correctly.
• Press CONTINUE to allow automatic sizing/calibration, then press START to initiate
compressions.
• Confirm the band remains centered after any movement or transfer.
• If the device alarms or cannot be corrected immediately, remove the patient from the device and
resume manual CPR.
• The infinity sign button should be lighted to provide continuous compressions.

Equipment:
1. Chlorhexidine/isopropanol swab
2. Jet ventilation catheter
3. Oxygen source
4. BVM
5. Mask with securing straps
6. Meconium aspirator
7. Suction tubing
8. ETCO2 adaptor
Procedure:
9. Hyperextend the neck of the patient. It might be helpful to place a pillow under the patient’s
neck
10. Remove the Jet Ventilation Catheter from the packaging
a. A syringe, attached to the catheter, serves as a handle and for identification for
correct positioning of the catheter
11. Locate the cricothyroid membrane by palpation of the depression between the thyroid and
cricoid cartilage
a. Stabilize this point with index finger and thumb for puncture
12. Puncture the cricothyroid membrane
a. Because of the sharp tip and conical shape of the needle, an incision is not necessary
b. After perforation of the cricothyroid membrane, a loss of resistance can be felt
13. Aspirate air with the syringe to determine the position of the catheter
a. If this is possible, the needle is in the trachea
b. The metal needle must not be introduced further
14. Push the catheter forward along the needle until the flange rests on the neck
a. Once in the trachea, the metal needle must NOT be introduced further to avoid
perforation of the rear tracheal wall
b. The metal needle serves as a guide and prevents kinking of the catheter
15. Now the metal needle can be removed
a. For safety reasons, check the correct positioning again by aspiration of air via a
syringe
b. If applicable, fill the syringe with 2 - 3 ml sterile saline solution
16. Secure device utilizing the supplied neck strap but continue to hold position manually.
17. Connect the suction tubing and meconium aspirator to an oxygen source
a. Set flow rate at 12 - 15 LPM
18. Cover mouth and nose with a BVM/CPAP mask and secure with straps
19. Place ETCO2 adapter on the mask
a. Cover hole on mask / ETCO2 adaptor simultaneously with the hole on the meconium
aspirator to provide insufflation - until you see chest rise.

Procedure
Hyperextend the neck of the patient. It might be helpful to place a pillow under the patient’s neck
Remove the Jet Ventilation Catheter from the packaging
A syringe, attached to the catheter, serves as a handle and for identification for correct positioning of the catheter
Locate the cricothyroid membrane by palpation of the depression between the thyroid and cricoid cartilage
Stabilize this point with index finger and thumb for puncture
Puncture the cricothyroid membrane
Because of the sharp tip and conical shape of the needle, an incision is not necessary
After perforation of the cricothyroid membrane, a loss of resistance can be felt
Aspirate air with the syringe to determine the position of the catheter
If this is possible, the needle is in the trachea
The metal needle must not be introduced further
Push the catheter forward along the needle until the flange rests on the neck
Once in the trachea, the metal needle must NOT be introduced further to avoid perforation of the rear tracheal wall
The metal needle serves as a guide and prevents kinking of the catheter
Now the metal needle can be removed
For safety reasons, check the correct positioning again by aspiration of air via a syringe
If applicable, fill the syringe with 2 - 3 ml sterile saline solution
Secure device utilizing the supplied neck strap but continue to hold position manually.
Connect the suction tubing and meconium aspirator to an oxygen source
Set flow rate at 12 - 15 LPM

Equipment:
1. Enhanced ARS (10 gauge 3.25”) needle
a. 16- or 18-gauge IV catheter (for infants and small children)
Landmarks:
2. 2nd intercostal space at the mid-clavicular line
a. The 2nd rib attaches to the sternum at the manubriosternal junction (Angle of
Louis)
3. 4th or 5th intercostal space, lateral to the nipple or inframammary crease, between the
anterior and mid-axillary line
a. If site can be difficult to evaluate, err to the next rib level superior
Procedure:
4. Prep the site with chlorhexidine/isopropanol swab. Open the needle set. Avoid touching
the sterile catheter to be inserted, unless wearing sterile gloves
5. Insert the catheter while attempting to contact the superior aspect of the rib
a. If rib contact, make note of needle depth at skin level with needle / rib contact
6. Withdraw slightly to disengage contact with rib and continue insertion just above the rib
at the chosen site until you feel a “pop”, decreased resistance to needle advancement,
or a rush of air as the tension is relieved
7. Stabilize needle in position and thread catheter into pleural space
a. If unable to thread catheter into chest, maintain needle/catheter engagement
b. Insert needle and catheter further and then make another attempt to thread
catheter into pleural space
c. IF needle has been inserted to a depth of 3cm beyond depth measured
when rib contact was made, and still UNABLE to thread off needle and
into chest, reassess landmarks and placement
8. After catheter threaded into chest, remove needle, leaving catheter in place and
place one-way valve
9. If tension reoccurs, repeat needle decompression, or perform a finger thoracostomy

Equipment:

a. Small: hip circumference of 27” – 45”
b. Standard: hip circumference of 32” – 50”

Procedure:
2. Assess the pelvic area, distal circulation, sensation, and motor function of lower

7. Maintain tension and immediately press the black strap onto the surface of the SAM
splint to secure

extremities q 15 minutes
a. Document findings in your PCR

blocks.text:
Equipment:
• Surgical mask and eye shield
• Chlorhexidine prep (or similar)
• Enhanced ARS 3.25” 10-gauge needle
• 30 - 60 mL syringe with Luer lock
• 3-way stopcock
Procedure:
1. Formally announce the procedure will be performed and brief all team members
a. Move the patient as able to optimize operator position, lighting, and safety
b. Monitor ECG, SpO2, respiratory rate, NIBP, and capnography
2. Perform a kit dump and set up equipment in a stable secure area
a. Open packaging just enough to facilitate access but maintain sterility and cleanliness
b. Attach the needle to the syringe
3. Don mask and eye protection
4. Expose and prepare the lower chest and upper abdomen
a. Cleanse the lower chest and upper abdomen with chlorhexidine or comparable
surgical scrub
b. Locate the insertion site left of the xiphoid and 1 cm inferior to the lower costal margin
5. Introduce the needle and aspirate fluid and blood
a. Have an assistant monitor the ECG and alert the operator if an ST elevation injury
pattern or ventricular ectopy occurs
b. Advance the needle slowly at a 30-degree angle to the skin aiming toward the posterior
left shoulder
c. Aspirate during needle advancement and monitor for fluid return
d. If no fluid is aspirated, withdraw the needle and redirect it systematically changing
posterior trajectory and left to right angles
e. Withdraw the needle if ST elevation injury pattern or ventricular ectopy occurs
indicating epicardial contact
f. Stop needle advancement when blood or fluid is present and advance catheter fully,
aspirate as much as possible
6. After initial aspiration, remove the needle leaving the catheter in place with a three-way
stopcock attached for future aspiration
a. Secure the catheter with tape

2. Pre-Oxygenation:
• Unless otherwise contraindicated, consider elevating the head of bed to 20° to enhance
oxygenation and nitrogen washout
• Initiate Pre-Oxygenation for at least 5 minutes:
o NRB @ flush rate, PLUS
o Standard nasal cannula at 15 LPM
• If the patient’s SpO2 remains ≤ 94% despite pre-oxygenation:
o Remove NRB and apply BVM with 10 PEEP, ensuring a tight mask fit to provide
CPAP effect.
o CPAP or BiPAP may also be used via ventilator or Flow-Safe II
o Consider Delayed Sequence Intubation
• Delayed Sequence Intubation (DSI) may be considered if the patient is combative or
otherwise unable to tolerate pre-oxygenation procedure.
o Administer ketamine 1mg/kg if the patient is agitated or will not tolerate mask
and fully prepare for RSI to facilitate use of BVM/CPAP.
o Time between the two ketamine administrations should be used to optimize
oxygenation (positioning, increased FiO2, etc…). This process may take a few
minutes.
o Prior to paralysis and intubation, the patient should receive an additional 1 mg/kg
of ketamine to reach the full induction dose of 2 mg/kg and ensure sedation
3. Pre-Intubation Optimization:
• If hypotensive (SBP <110 in head injuries and <90 for all others), you MUST
hemodynamically resuscitate the patient prior to administering any RSI medications, as
they can cause cardiac depression and/or a decrease in sympathetic tone leading to
further hypotension and/or cardiac arrest, especially when PPV is provided to the patient.
o Rapid fluid bolus: hypotension from dehydration, sepsis, etc.
o Blood (if available): hypotension from bleeding.
o Vasopressors: push dose Epinephrine for hypotension refractory to fluids/blood or
if you need an immediate increase in BP.
o Chest decompression for known or suspected tension pneumothorax
o Induction agent: use half dose Ketamine or Midazolam
o Shock index (HR / SBP), positive if:
i. Age ≥ 13: > 0.9
ii. Age 7 – 12: > 1.0
iii. Age 4 – 6: > 1.22
4. Pre-Treatment:
• If age ≤ 28 days
o Atropine 0.02 mg/kg IV
• If using midazolam for induction of a pediatric patient
o Fentanyl 2 mcg/kg IV

5. Prepare Medications:
Sedatives
• Ketamine 1-2 mg/kg IV3,4
o Wait at least 30 seconds after administration before giving a paralytic
o Drug of choice for most patients
o Use lower dose for hypotensive patients
• Etomidate 0.3 mg/kg IV May repeat x2.
o Administer the paralytic immediately after administering etomidate
o Max adult dose: 40 mg
o Max pediatric dose: 20 mg
o You must have post intubation sedation and analgesia medications drawn up and
ready to administer due to the short duration of etomidate
• Midazolam 0.2 mg/kg IV
o Pediatric dose: 0.1 mg/kg
o Max dose 20 mg
o Caution in hypotensive patients
o Wait three minutes after administration before giving paralytic
Paralytics
• Succinylcholine 1 – 2 mg/kg IV
o Max 200 mg, do not repeat dose
o First line agent unless patient is < 10 years or has other contraindications, see
formulary for more information.
o Avoid if potassium level is ≥ 6 mEq/L
• Rocuronium 1 mg/kg IV or 2 mg/kg IM
o Max 100 mg
6. Placement with Proof:
• Once patient is paralyzed, perform intubation
o Consider utilizing external laryngeal manipulation and/or Backward Upward
Rightward Pressure (BURP) to improve glottic visualization1,2
• Stop intubation attempt if SpO2 drops <90%.
o Re-oxygenate the patient with 100% oxygen PLUS 5 – 10 cmH20 PEEP via BVM
prior to attempting again. Consider making a change in technique or equipment.
o If bradycardia persists despite adequate re-oxygenation:
i. STOP attempt
ii. Administer atropine
1. Adult: 1 mg IV q 3 – 5 min to max of 3 mg
2. Pediatric: 0.02 mg/kg IV q 3 – 5 min
• Maximum of two intubation attempts per team member
o If intubation attempts fail, re-oxygenate the patient prior to
additional attempts and/or consider alternate airway placement
(SGA or cricothyrotomy)

• ETCO2 is mandatory with all intubations (ETT and SGA).
o In situations where there is not a consistent ETCO2 waveform, confirm ETT
placement via recorded video laryngoscopy with validation by another partner (at
each patient movement) -OR- the ETT should be removed and ventilation
performed by alternate methods.
• In addition to ETCO2, verify placement by at least two separate techniques:
o Auscultate for bilateral breath sounds and absent gastric sounds
o Observe for equal chest rise and fall
o Maintenance or increase in SpO2
o Misting of tube
• Secure tube at proper depth with a commercial device
o It is best to visualize ETT depth, passing the balloon approximately 1 cm past the
vocal cords or placing the cord marker at the vocal cords.
o Otherwise, approximate ETT depth at the incisors or anterior alveolar ridge (in cm)
i. Patients ≥ 5 feet (60 inches): (height in inches/4) + 4
ii. Patients < 5 feet tall: 3 X ETT size
7. Post Intubation Management
• Use the ETT cuff manometer to check cuff pressures
o Adult target: 20 – 25 cmH2O
o Pediatric target: 15 – 20 cmH2O
• Consider placing a c-collar to help maintain tube placement, especially on pediatric
patients
• Place the patient on a ventilator for transport, regardless of estimated transport time
• Maintain sedation for patient comfort as well as crew and aircraft safety. See Pain
Management and Sedation guidelines
o Consider infusions for long transports
o Providing analgesia first can reduce the amount of sedation required
• It is not necessary to maintain paralysis on every patient but consider continued
paralysis for patients with a history of combativeness or agitation. Consider the
constraints of the aircraft/vehicle, patient size, and crew safety. For other patients,
consider using sedation only without ongoing paralysis
• To maintain paralysis, administer rocuronium 0.5 mg/kg IV
o Repeat q 30 min or more frequently PRN
• To initiate paralysis in the intubated patient who is no longer paralyzed, administer
rocuronium 1 mg/kg IV or 1.8mg/kg IM
• Consider NG/OG tube to facilitate ventilation
• Document the name of receiving physician who verified proper placement of ETT before
finalizing the clinical chart
o Do not document the procedure was “successful” without documenting the name
of the physician who verified placement
o If the crew is told their placement was incorrect, immediately notify the Clinical
Manager on Call (CMOC) and complete a QM report

laryngoscope

freeing the laryngoscopist’s right hand to place the tube

3. Laryngospasm:
a. If during intubation, stop the procedure
b. Apply a tight-fitting mask and ventilate with 100% oxygen via a BVM with 10
cmH2O PEEP
c. Simultaneously perform the Larson’s maneuver
i. Standing at the patient’s head, place the middle finger of each hand in the
notch behind the patient’s earlobe
ii. Press firmly inward and upward toward the base of the skull
iii. Simultaneously lift the mandible with your index fingers (jaw thrust)
d. If laryngospasm persists, ensure patient has received ketamine 2 mg/kg,
administer paralytic agent and intubate immediately
4. Increased muscle tone with tonic and clonic movements resembling seizures
a. Occurs with initial dose and gradually decreases
b. Typically, does not affect chest wall or respiration
c. Treatment rarely needed, but consider benzodiazepines or paralytic and
intubation PRN
d. Ketamine may be re-dosed as needed as this is not an allergic reaction, not a true
seizure, and typically does not recur

Simultaneously perform the Larson’s maneuver
Standing at the patient’s head, place the middle finger of each hand in the notch behind the patient’s earlobe
Press firmly inward and upward toward the base of the skull
Simultaneously lift the mandible with your index fingers (jaw thrust)

Increased muscle tone with tonic and clonic movements resembling seizures
Occurs with initial dose and gradually decreases
Typically, does not affect chest wall or respiration
Treatment rarely needed, but consider benzodiazepines or paralytic and intubation PRN
Ketamine may be re-dosed as needed as this is not an allergic reaction, not a true seizure, and typically does not recur 5.

Advanced airway transfers: disconnect ventilator/BVETT if tolerated; verify ETT/SGA securement in commercial holder prior to movement; confirm placement with ETCO₂ immediately after each transfer to prevent risk of unplanned extubation.

Equipment:
1. Cervical collar
2. Webbing or quick-release belts (duct tape is discouraged)
3. Scoop (preferred) or backboard, and/or stretcher
4. Head securing method
Procedure:
1. Perform spinal motion restriction (SMR) assessment. If ANY of the following are present,
apply SMR:
a. Altered mental status
b. Evidence of intoxication
c. Midline neck and/or back pain and/or tenderness
d. Focal neurologic deficits or symptoms
e. Anatomic deformity of the spine
f. Distracting injury or circumstance, including extreme agitation or emotional
distress
g. Torticollis in children (may require immobilization in position found)
h. A communication barrier that prevents accurate assessment
i. Increased suspicion of spinal injury by provider (mechanism of injury, age, etc.)
2. If SMR is indicated:
a. Patient is reliable and ambulatory on-scene or can safely self-extricate:
i. Place cervical collar on patient. Direct patient to limit spine movement
ii. Allow the patient to move him or herself to the unloaded stretcher
iii. Secure the patient to the stretcher
iv. Transport the patient in a supine position or position of comfort
v. Upon arrival at the hospital, assist the patient in moving to the hospital’s
stretcher. If any pain experienced, use a slide board to maintain spinal
alignment.
3. If the patient has altered mental status, intoxication, a distracting injury or circumstance,
a communication barrier, is unreliable, requires extrication, or is not ambulatory:
a. Place cervical collar on patient. Direct patient to limit spine movement
b. Use a scoop or backboard as needed to move patient to the stretcher
c. Remove backboard or scoop once the patient is on the stretcher, maintaining in-
line spinal alignment. Secure the patient to the stretcher. The patient may remain
on the backboard or scoop if moving would otherwise delay critical
interventions/rapid transport
d. Transport the patient in a supine position
e. Upon arrival at the hospital, move the patient to the hospital stretcher while
maintaining inline spinal alignment with a slide board

Spinal Motion
Restriction

1. Consider extremes of age and the cognitive ability of the patient to understand
assessment question
2. Patients ≥65 years old are more prone to skeletal injury with even minimal traumatic
insult
3. Patients must clearly understand the language spoken AND must have the cognitive
ability to comprehend the answers asked in the SMR assessment
4. Immobilized patients are at high risk for aspiration secondary to nausea/vomiting or
blood in the mouth
5. Assess adequacy of respirations in all immobilized patients. Avoid placing securing
devices over the abdomen of pediatric patients
6. Ensure proper padding under the shoulders to maintain neutral alignment in pediatric
patients
7. Limit the motion of the spine in any patient movement
8. If in doubt, apply SMR and/or contact Medical Consult
9. The determination of the need for continued immobilization during transport is to be
made by the sending provider in consultation with the receiving physician. However, due
to the risk of pressure sores/decubitus ulcers, the patient should be transported
immobilized on the LFN stretcher without a hard backboard whenever possible
10. It is acceptable to use the hard backboard if the patient is already immobilized and flight
time is < 20 minutes
11. If utilized, placement on the hard backboard should be performed as late as possible
and the backboard should be padded with a blanket or Back-Raft whenever possible
12. There may be some cases in which the physician “clears” the lumbar/thoracic spine but
still maintains cervical immobilization. These patients may be immobilized on the LFN
stretcher without a backboard if they are cooperative and able to protect their airway.

Equipment:
1. Chlorhexidine/isopropanol swab
2. Bougie
3. #10 scalpel
4. Ruiz Hook
5. Sterile gauze pads
6. Twill tape
7. Suction

Prepare
Palpate / Identify
4. Palpate the neck in the midline and locate the slight depression just below the inferior
border of the thyroid cartilage and just above the cricoid cartilage.
a. This is the cricothyroid membrane.
b. Approximate location is three to four finger breadths (patient’s fingers) above the
sternal notch.
c. IF you are UNABLE to IDENTIFY the cricothyroid membrane, make a 2” vertical
incision over the suspected location, then dissect until you are able to
palpate/locate the membrane.
Stabilize
5. If you are ABLE to IDENTIFY the cricothyroid membrane by palpation:
a. STABILIZE the airway by stretching skin across the thyroid cartilage or by
maintaining grasp on the thyroid cartilage with your non-dominate hand.
b. Best practice is to use your thumb and long finger to allow palpation of the site
with your index finger.
c. Make a small, pinpoint incision over the site with the top of the scalpel.
6. Puncture the membrane with the Ruiz hook, then hook along the inferior edge of the
thyroid cartilage and lift toward the head.

Equipment:

Procedure:
1. Removal all clothing covering the patient’s chest
a. Dry chest if necessary
b. If the patient has excessive chest hair, clip or shave it to ensure proper adhesion of
the electrodes
2. Attach ECG electrodes
a. A standard ECG cable and ECG electrodes are recommended for use during
cardioversion
b. Hands-free therapy electrodes may be used as an ECG source.1
3. Attach hands-free therapy electrodes – AP is the preferred placement location
a. Ensure that the therapy electrodes are making good contact with the patient’s skin
and are not covering any part of any other electrodes
4. Consider procedural sedation for alert patients
5. Press the Sync quick access key on the front panel. The system will now be in SYNC mode
a. A sync marker (S) appears on the monitor above each detected R-wave to indicate
where discharge will occur
b. A Sync indicator appears at the top of the display screen, and a green light next to the
indicator flashes with each Sync marker
6. Unless otherwise configured, the unit automatically exits Sync mode after each shock
a. To reactivate SYNC mode, press the Sync quick access key on the front panel again
7. Changing the selected energy levels does not cause the unit to leave SYNC mode
8. Press the Energy Select arrows up or down to select the desired energy level
9. Press the CHARGE button on the front panel
a. To increase or decrease the selected energy after you have pressed the CHARGE
button, use the defibrillator Energy Select arrows on the front panel
10. Warn all persons in attendance of the patient to STAND CLEAR prior to defibrillator discharge
a. Verify that no one is in contact with the patient, monitoring cable or leads, bed rails, or
any other potential current pathways
11. Press and hold the illuminated SHOCK button on the front panel until energy is delivered to
the patient
a. The defibrillator will discharge with the next detected R wave
b. Unless otherwise configured, the unit automatically exits Sync mode after each
shock
c. To reactivate SYNC mode, press the Sync quick access key on the front panel again
d. Changing the selected energy levels does not cause the unit to leave SYNC mode

4. Set Mode
a. Use the arrow keys to navigate to Mode, press the Select button, and then use the
arrow keys and the Select button to set the Pacer Mode to Demand
5. Set Rate
a. Use the arrow keys to navigate to Rate, press the Select button, and then use the
arrow keys and the Select button to set the Pacer Rate to a value 10-20 ppm
higher than the patient’s intrinsic heart rate. If no intrinsic rate exists, use 80 ppm.
b. You can increase or decrease the pacer rate by a value of 5 ppm for rates below
100, and by 10 ppm for rates above 100.
6. Turn on Pacer
a. Use the arrow keys to navigate to Start Pacer, then press the Select button to
select it. The Pacing window (below) displays behind the Pacer Settings window.
7. Set Pacer Output (mA)
a. In the Pacer Settings window, use the arrow keys and the Select button to adjust
the pacer output
b. Typical threshold ranges from 40 – 80 mA
c. The pacer output is adjustable in 10 mA increments when increasing the output,
and in 5 mA increments when decreasing the output.
d. Observe the ECG for evidence of electrical capture.
e. Select the lowest output current that achieves both electrical and mechanical
capture.
f. If the Pacer Settings window disappears before you have set the output current,
press the PACER button again to display the settings window
8. Determine Capture
a. It is important to recognize when pacing stimulation has produced a ventricular
response (capture).
b. Determination of capture must be assessed both electrically and mechanically in
order to ensure appropriate circulatory support of the patient.
i. Electrical capture is determined by the presence of a widened QRS
complex, the loss of any underlying intrinsic rhythm, and the appearance
of an extended, and sometimes enlarged, T-wave. Ventricular response is
normally characterized by suppression of the intrinsic QRS complex.
ii. Mechanical capture is assessed by palpation of the peripheral pulse. To
avoid mistaking muscular response to pacing stimuli for arterial
pulsations, use ONLY the following locations for palpating pulse during
pacing:
a. Femoral artery
b. Right brachial or radial artery
9. Changing ECG leads and size can sometimes be helpful in determining capture
a. The shape and size of the paced ECG waveforms can vary depending on the ECG
lead configuration chosen; variation from patient to patient can be expected.

• Do Not Resuscitate
o If any of the following are present:
▪ A pulseless, apneic patient in a mass casualty incident (MCI) or multiple patient
scene where the resources of the system are required for the stabilization of living
patients
▪ Decapitation
▪ Rigor mortis in a warm environment
▪ Decomposition
▪ Skin discoloration in dependent body parts (dependent lividity)
▪ Pulseless and apneic with a valid Do Not Resuscitate (DNR) order
▪ Idaho, Oregon, Montana, or Washington POLST (Physician Orders for Life Sustaining
Treatment)
▪ Signed DNR order from another state
o Special Considerations:
▪ Most victims of electrocution, lightning, and drowning should have resuscitative
efforts initiated and be transported to an appropriate hospital
o Notes:
▪ Crews may transport a patient who would normally have resuscitation terminated at
the scene if deemed appropriate for safety or compassion issues (e.g., gang related
violence, pediatrics, etc.)
▪ Oregon patients: If an original POLST cannot be produced, contact the POLST
Registry at (877) 367-7657.
• Upon confirmation of patient identity, the Registry can relay Section A and B
POLST orders. Registry staff do not interpret orders
▪ Hospital DNR orders are not valid outside of the hospital
▪ Death of Pre-Established Hospice Patients:
▪ If the patient dies during transport, the crew may continue to their home or hospice
facility and place them into the bed or location of the family’s choice.
▪ The family will notify the hospice facility (if the decedent is taken to a home) to take
care of notifying the ME and other details.
• POLST orders and decision making
o In the pulseless and apneic patient who does not meet DEATH IN THE FIELD criteria but is
suspected to be a candidate for withholding resuscitation, begin CPR and contact OLMC
o A patient with decision-making capacity or the legally authorized representative has the
right to direct his or her own medical care and can change or rescind previous directives
o EMS providers may honor a POLST Do Not Attempt Resuscitation (DNAR) order signed by a
physician, naturopathic physician, nurse practitioner, or physician assistant
o DNAR orders apply only to the patient in cardiopulmonary arrest and do not indicate the
types of treatment that a person not in arrest should receive. POLST was developed to
convey orders in other circumstances
o Remember DNR does not mean do not treat
CONTINUES TO NEXT PAGE
Death In
The Field
o The POLST was developed to document and communicate patient treatment preferences
across treatment settings.
▪ While these forms are most often used to limit care, they may also indicate that the
patient wants everything medically appropriate done
▪ Read the form carefully!
o When signed by a physician (MD or DO), naturopathic physician, nurse practitioner, or
physician assistant, POLST is a medical order and EMS providers are directed to honor it in
their Scope of Practice unless they have reason to doubt the validity of the orders or the
patient with decision making capacity requests change
▪ If there are questions regarding the validity or enforceability of the health care
instruction, begin BLS treatment and contact OLMC [OAR 847-035-030 (7)]
o If the POLST is not immediately available, a POLST form as documented in the Electronic
POLST registry hosted at MRH (503-494-7333) may also be honored
▪ Section A: Applies only when patient is in cardiopulmonary arrest
▪ Section B: Applies in all other circumstances
o For a POLST form to be valid, it must include
▪ Patient’s name
▪ Date signed (forms do not expire)
▪ Health care professional’s signature (patient signature is optional)
o The legally authorized representative may make decisions for the patient who is unable to
make medical decisions. However, when in doubt or for unresolved conflict on the scene
contact OLMC. The order is:
▪ A legal guardian
▪ A power of attorney for health care as designated by the patient on the Oregon
advance directive.
▪ Spouse or legal domestic partner
▪ Adult children
▪ Parent
• Care of Grieving Persons
o Resuscitation Phase:
▪ As time allows, give accurate and truthful updates about the patient’s prognosis. If
available, assign one person to interact with and support family members.
▪ Depending upon the emotional state of family members, consider allowing them to
watch and/or participate in a limited and appropriate way.
▪ Be respectful. Make requests. Don’t give orders.
CONTINUES TO NEXT PAGE
Death In
The Field
• Once Death is Determined
o Treat the recently dead with respect
o Tell family and friends of the death honestly. Use the words “death” or “dead.” Avoid using
euphemisms such as “passed away” or “gone”
o Avoid using past tense terms when speaking to survivors of the recently dead
o Allow family and friends to express their emotions
▪ Listen to them if they want to talk but don’t push them
o Give factual information
o Genuine warmth and compassion will be more helpful than almost anything else for
survivors
▪ Don’t feel it necessary to say the “right” things. Listening often provides grieving
people with the most comfort
• Focusing on Survivors
o See to it that survivors have a support system present before you leave.
▪ Consider calling friends, family, clergy, or neighbors to be with them.
▪ Respect the survivors’ wishes to be alone.
o Explain the next steps to them after you have pronounced death.
▪ This will include the police coming to make reports, possibly the medical examiner,
and the possible need for an autopsy
o Before moving or altering the body, contact the Medical Examiner’s office as soon as
possible
o Allow family and friends to say their good-byes if possible
o Help survivors make decisions such as which people should be called. If they ask you to
make calls, try to comply.
▪ Mention the need to find a funeral home if one has not been chosen
o Clergy may also be helpful with this decision
• Death of a Child
o Do not be overly silent, which may imply guilt to the parents
o Ask the parents only necessary questions and do not judge or evaluate them
▪ Do not tell them what they “should have” been doing before your arrival
o Remind parents to arrange for childcare of other children, if applicable
o Listen carefully to their statements and answer with accurate information
o Successful management of child deaths requires supportive, compassionate, and tactful
measure

1. Patient destination on scene calls should be determined utilizing several factors:
a) Statewide Destination protocols
b) Patient preference
c) Direction by local EMS providers or protocols, and/or via Online Medical Control
d) In the absence of these factors, patients should generally be transported to the closest
appropriate facility based upon the patient’s illness and condition
2. Level I and II trauma facilities both provide definitive care for severely injured patients, with Level I
facilities also providing trauma education and research
3. In cases where transport destinations are not addressed in Statewide Protocols or these
Guidelines, and transport time to the hospital offering definitive care exceeds the closest hospital
by >30 minutes, strongly consider contacting the closest facility for advice regarding the
appropriate destination
4. Unstable patients may benefit from stabilization at the closest facility before transferring to the
facility offering definitive care
5. The presence of an extremity tourniquet is significant to trauma leveling.
a) If the patient has a tourniquet, please include this as part of your pre arrival report to
ensure proper trauma team response
6. When a patient and/or family member requests transport to a facility that deviates from local
protocols or these Guidelines:
a) Assess medical decision-making capacity. See Refusal of Treatment.
b) A patient with decision-making capacity or their family may request a destination facility of
their choosing, but they must be provided enough information regarding the risks and
benefits to make an informed decision
c) If the patient requests a facility more than 25 NM beyond the closest appropriate facility,
advise them we will honor the request, but their insurance may not cover the additional
cost. We want them to make an informed decision
7. If, in your opinion, the patient makes a less-than-optimal choice after weighing the information
provided, consider online medical control, and have the patient sign a refusal in order to
document your plan to take them to the closest appropriate facility
8. The sending provider shall determine patient destination for interfacility transfers
a) In accordance with EMTALA, the sending provider is responsible for ensuring the patient
transfer is appropriate
9. For flights originating in the State of Idaho, the following guidelines and practices will be in effect:
a) Transport prehospital patients in accordance with local EMS air ambulance protocols
when applicable
b) St. Luke’s has obtained their Level II Pediatric Trauma Center designation from the
American College of Surgeons.
▪ Level 1 and 2 pediatric traumas can go to St. Luke’s preferentially

Washington Stroke Triage Destination Procedure
The purpose of the Prehospital Stroke Triage and Destination Procedure is to identify stroke patients in
the field and take them to the most appropriate hospital, which might not be the nearest hospital.
Stroke treatment is time-critical – the sooner patients are treated, the better their chances of survival
and recovering function.
For strokes caused by a blocked blood vessel in the brain (ischemic, the majority of strokes), clot-
busting medication (tPA) must be administered within 4.5 hours from the time the patient was last known
well, a treatment that can be given at WA DOH Level 1, 2 or 3 stroke centers (for a list of categorized
hospitals, please click here).
If a patient presents to EMS with a severe stroke, they are more likely to have blockage of a large
vessel and can benefit from mechanical clot retrieval (thrombectomy). Thrombectomy must begin by 24
hours since last known well, and is a more complex intervention, only available in Level I and a
small number of Level II stroke centers.
There are 3 key elements to determine the appropriate destination hospital:
1. FAST stroke screen to identify a patient with a high probability of stroke
2. Stroke Severity Score to determine if a patient meets criteria for “severe” stroke
3. Time since Last Known Well (LKW) which helps determine eligibility for tPA and thrombectomy
STEPS to determine destination:
1. Do a FAST Stroke Screen Assessment: (facial droop, arm drift, speech changes, time since (LKW)
is a simple way to tell if someone might be having a stroke.
a. If FAST is negative, stroke is less likely, and standard destination procedures apply.
b. If FAST is positive (face or arms or speech is abnormal), it’s likely the patient is having a
stroke, and the EMS provider moves on to assessing stroke severity
2. Assess severity: The stroke severity assessment scores the FAST stroke screen. Patients get
points for deficits:
a. Facial droop:
i. 1 point if present
ii. 0 points if absent
b. Arm drift (have patient hold arms up in air):
i. 2 points if an arm falls rapidly
ii. 1 point if slowly drifts down

Purpose
The National Guideline for Field Triage of Injured Patients was developed by a
multidisciplinary panel led by the American College of Surgeons Committee on Trauma. The
guideline has been adopted by the Department of Health (DOH) based on the recommendation of
the State Emergency Medical Services (EMS) and Trauma Steering Committee in association with
the Prehospital and Hospital Technical Advisory Committees.
The guideline represents the current best practice for the triage of trauma patients and
allows EMS providers to quickly and accurately determine if the casualty is a major or moderate
trauma patient. It also aids in decision making to determine the most appropriate transfer facility
location.
The triage procedure is described below in Figure 1. It consolidates triage criteria into two
main categories based on risk of serious injury: High-Risk Criteria (red box) includes Injury
Patterns, Mental Status, and Vital Signs. Moderate-Risk Criteria (yellow box) includes
Mechanism of Injury and EMS Judgment. Each risk category is aligned with recommendations for
a destination trauma service. Figure 1. is intended to be read from top to bottom, left to right.
Any certified EMS provider can identify a major trauma patient and alert receiving
hospitals. Hospitals will activate their trauma team based on their internal policies and
procedures. EMS providers should follow regional Patient Care Procedures (PCPs) and County
Operating Procedures (COPs) for engaging other system partners such as air ambulance and
advanced level ground ambulance services to coordinate the most appropriate and expedient
transport modality for a trauma patient.
Red Criteria / High Risk for Serious Injury
Assess Injury Patterns, Mental Status & Vital Signs
Assessment of injury patterns, mental status, and vital signs meeting red criteria should
require alerting and rapidly transporting to the closest level I or II trauma service within 30
minutes transport time. If the transport time is greater than 30 minutes, transfer should be to the
nearest most appropriate trauma service.
If unable to maintain a patent airway, consider rendezvous with an Advanced Life Support
(ALS) unit or transporting to the nearest facility capable of definitive airway management. The
presence of specific injury patterns with normal vital signs, lack of pain, or normal levels of
consciousness; requires calling medical control and alerting the receiving hospital. Pediatric
patients meeting the red criteria should be preferentially triaged to designated pediatric trauma
service.
Yellow Criteria / Moderate Risk for Serious Injury
Assess Mechanism of Injury and EMS Judgement
An assessment of the mechanism of injury meeting yellow criteria should require alerting
and rapidly transporting to the closest appropriate trauma service within 30 minutes (air or
ground). The destination trauma service need not be the highest-level trauma service. Risk factors
coupled with "provider judgment" are reasons for the provider to contact Medical Control and
discuss appropriate destinations for these patients.
