Determination
In some cases, the decision may be to transport to the nearest trauma service or a
resource hospital. Patients with combined burns and trauma should be preferentially transported
to a trauma center with burn care capability. Pediatric patients should be preferentially
transported to a designated pediatric trauma service.
PCPs and local COPs provide additional details about the appropriate hospital destination.

needs.

1. In all cases, when a physician on scene offers to provide assistance and/or medical direction, Life
Flight Network personnel will determine the physician’s identity and medical specialty
a. A physician on scene may not provide assistance and/or medical direction unless the
following conditions are met:
2. The physician must be currently licensed to practice medicine in the state where the scene is
located
a. The physician’s medical specialty must be pertinent to the patient’s medical condition
b. The physician agrees to accompany the patient to the hospital (subject to pilot approval for
fixed wing or rotor transports) and understands they are responsible for any and all care
given
c. The physician agrees to sign a copy of the LFN Patient Care Record as soon as possible
(see #6, below)
d. When possible, contact OLMC or the Life Flight Network Medical Director to speak with the
on-scene physician regarding their offer of assistance or care
3. The following physicians are exempt from this policy provided they are licensed to practice
medicine in the state in which the call occurs:
a. Life Flight Network Medical Directors
b. The patient’s attending physician
4. At no time will Life Flight Network personnel render care outside their scope of practice and
training at the direction of a physician on scene, including those listed in number 3 above
5. If during transport, the patient’s condition should warrant treatment other than that requested by
the attending physician, on-line medical control or a Life Flight Network Medical Director must be
contacted for advice and concurrence
6. Because of the nature of our electronic charting process, an event log entry must be completed to
fully document the circumstances of an on-scene physician assuming patient control. This event
log will contain at a minimum:
a. The physician’s name
b. Address
c. Phone number
d. License number
e. Specialty
f. All orders carried out at the direction of the physician
g. A statement indicating the physician was physically present during all times once they
assumed control, including:
i. Accompanying the patient to the receiving hospital, and
ii. That the physician verbally agreed to sign a copy of the electronic chart as soon as
practical
7. The electronic chart containing the original signature of the physician will be maintained at the
Life Flight Network administrative offices for a period not less than 25 years
8. Upon completion of a transport of this nature, immediately notify the Life Flight Network Medical
Director and the Clinical Manager On Call (CMOC)
9. A Quality Management (QM) report will be completed any time a physician assumes or attempts
to assume medical control

A physician on scene may not provide assistance and/or medical direction unless the
following conditions are met
The physician must be currently licensed to practice medicine in the state where the scene is located
The physician’s medical specialty must be pertinent to the patient’s medical condition
The physician agrees to accompany the patient to the hospital (subject to pilot approval for fixed wing or rotor transports) and understands they are responsible for any and all care given
The physician agrees to sign a copy of the LFN Patient Care Record as soon as possible (see #6, below)

Life Flight Network Medical Directors
The patient’s attending physician

blocks.text:
1. Our goal is to transport and appropriately treat all individuals who require our service
a. This goal notwithstanding, we will encounter individuals who will refuse a particular
treatment, air transport, or our services altogether
2. Assess and document medical decision-making capacity
a. Patients with reasonable medical decision-making capacity may refuse care if they
understand the consequences
3. Patient-initiated refusals of care must be documented in the patient care record
a. LFN 201.07 “Refusal of Treatment Form, Addendum A” will be used to document any
incident when a patient refuses a treatment recommended by the clinical crew, refuses air
transport, or refuses transport altogether
4. Findings that suggest reasonable medical decision-making capacity include:
a. Normal or near-normal vital signs
b. Normal level of consciousness
c. Normal orientation or orientation at usual baseline
d. Absence or minimal use of intoxicants
e. Coherent, non-pressured speech
f. Appropriate insight
g. Understanding of the risks of refusal
i. The patient needs to be able to reiterate these risks when asked
5. The following types of patients may not refuse care and should be transported to the closest
appropriate facility:
a. Intentional overdose
b. Attempted or threatened suicide
c. Grossly intoxicated
d. Minor*
e. Inadequate medical decision-making capacity
f. For aviation safety reasons, consider sedation or RSI when the patient cannot refuse care
and is agitated or combative
6. “Patients are allowed to make poor choices”
a. Nonetheless, Life Flight Network personnel may, in their role as patient advocate and in
certain patient-specific situations, elect to speak with the patient’s family and/or friends to
enlist their help in convincing the patient to accept medical care
i. The patient’s privacy and HIPAA rights must be protected during this conversation.
7. Whenever possible, it is preferable to have the individual who is refusing transport altogether
speak directly with a physician via on-line medical control
8. *The following minors are considered emancipated (state dependent) and may refuse treatment
and sign the refusal of treatment form:
a. Oregon: patients under 18 years of age are considered emancipated if they are:
i. Married, or
ii. Emancipated by court order
b. Washington: patients under 18 years of age are considered emancipated if they are:
i. Married to a person aged 18 or older, or
ii. Emancipated by court order
CONTINUES TO NEXT PAGE
Refusal of Treatment
c. Idaho: patients under 18 years of age are considered emancipated if they:
a. Are or have been married, or
b. Are in the active military service
d. Montana: patients under 18 years of age are considered emancipated if they:
c. Are or have been married, or
d. Are emancipated by court order

blocks.text:
• The Safe Haven Act is intended to provide a safe alternative to parents who otherwise might
abandon their infant
o Note: Safe Haven Acts are state-specific and are detailed below
▪ Oregon, Montana, and Washington Safe Haven laws exclude EMS providers
(outside of fire departments) as accepting agencies
▪ Safe Haven Acts for Oregon, Montana and Washington are listed below as a
resource only
1. Idaho:
a. EMS personnel may respond to the scene for a “Safe Haven” request
i. Alternatively, EMS personnel may be presented with an infant at their base/quarters
b. Custodial parent can leave his/her baby, up to 30 (thirty) days old
c. Safe haven providers include:
i. Licensed hospitals
ii. Licensed physicians and staff working at their offices and clinics
iii. Advanced practice professional nurses, including certified nurse-midwives, clinical
nurse specialists, nurse practitioners, and certified registered nurse anesthetists
iv. Licensed physician assistants
v. Medical personnel certified as first responders, emergency medical technicians,
and paramedics
d. Confirm the parent is requesting a “Safe Haven” for the infant and the parent does not
intend to reclaim the infant.
e. Provide aid to protect and preserve the health and safety of the infant, including, but not
limited to, delivering the child to a hospital for care or treatment
f. If law enforcement is not en route or present at the scene, notify the LFN Communications
Center to send law enforcement to place the infant in protective custody
g. Do not ask for the identity of the parent
i. If known, keep the identity confidential
h. Accept voluntary information given by the parent regarding the health history of the parent
or the infant
i. Transport the infant to the hospital in a child safety seat or other appropriate infant restrain
device
j. Report any voluntary information to hospital personnel while keeping the identity of the
parent and infant confidential, if known
k. In the patient care record, document the primary impression as “Safe Haven”
l. More information may be requested from the Idaho CareLine at 211 or 800-926-2588
CONTINUES TO NEXT PAGE
Safe Haven
2. Oregon:
a. A parent can leave their infant provided:
i. The baby is 30 days of age or younger as determined to a reasonable degree of
medical certainty
ii. There is no evidence of abuse
iii. The parent is not required to provide their identity or the identity of the child
b. Safe haven providers include an agent, employee, physician, or other medical profession
working at:
i. Hospital
ii. Fire station
iii. Free standing birthing center
iv. Physician’s office
v. Sheriff’s office or police station
vi. NOTE: EMS providers (outside of fire departments) are not included
3. Montana:
a. A parent may surrender a newborn, defined as an infant whom a physician reasonably
believes to be no more than 30 days old
b. The parent cannot express an intent to return for the newborn
c. The child may be surrendered to an emergency services provider, including:
i. A uniformed or otherwise identifiable employee of a fire department, hospital, or
law enforcement agency, when the individual is on duty inside the premises of the
fire department, hospital, or law enforcement agency
ii. Any law enforcement officer who is in uniform or is otherwise identifiable
iii. NOTE: EMS providers (outside of fire departments) are not included
4. Washington:
a. A parent can leave a newborn, defined as, “a live human being who is younger than 72
hours old”
b. The newborn may be left with a qualified individual at an appropriate location
i. Qualified Individual:
1. Any person that the parent transferring the newborn reasonably believes is a
bona fide employee, volunteer, or medical staff member of the hospital who
represents to the parent transferring the newborn that he or she can and will
summon appropriate resources to meet the newborn's immediate needs
2. A firefighter, volunteer, or emergency medical technician at a fire station who
represents to the parent transferring the newborn that he or she can and will
summon appropriate resources to meet the newborn's immediate needs
ii. Appropriate Location:
1. The emergency department of a licensed hospital during the hours the
hospital is in operation
2. A fire station during its hours of operation and while fire personnel are present
3. A federally designated rural health clinic during its hours of operation
4. NOTE: EMS agencies (outside of fire departments) are not included

Termination of Resuscitation CANNOT be performed without an advanced airway in place and
waveform ETCO2
1. The following must be present in order to consider termination of resuscitation in medical arrest
patients without contacting OLMC.
a. An advanced airway in place AND confirmed with waveform ETCO2
b. Age ≥ 18 years
c. Not knowingly pregnant
d. Patent vascular access
e. No neurological responses present
f. No ROSC obtained at any point in resuscitation
g. No identified reversible causes present
h. ECG remains in asystole after 20 minutes of resuscitation that follows the appropriate AHA
and LFN guidelines
i. Verification of absent heart tones for at least 60 seconds
2. Resuscitation during transport should not be terminated if the transport time to the original
destination hospital or airport is < 15 minutes
a. To better permit evaluation of patient status to include pulses, heart sounds, and airway
status, all efforts should be made to transport the patient to a receiving hospital or
destination airport and unloaded from the aircraft before decision to terminate
resuscitation
b. If the transport time to the original destination hospital is > 15 min, resuscitation may be
terminated in patients in cardiopulmonary arrest who meet criteria per Death in the Field
with OLMC consult
c. If unable to contact OLMC and termination of resuscitation is within your state scope of
practice, you may terminate resuscitation, otherwise you should continue the transport.
i. Note GPS coordinate of aircraft at time resuscitation was terminated
d. ETCO2 and ECG strips showing the rhythm at time of termination in two different leads
must be obtained and uploaded to the PCR
3. The Clinical Manager on Call (CMOC) and the LFN Communications Center will be notified when
resuscitation efforts are terminated inside a LFN transport vehicle
4. The Communications Center will alert the appropriate Medical Examiner or Coroner as soon as
they are made aware resuscitation efforts have been terminated
a. Rotor Wing Aircraft:
i. Notify receiving facility of termination of efforts
ii. Continue transport to receiving facility
iii. If remainder of transport is expected to be >30 min, contact the CMOC for
guidance.
iv. The body should be left in the aircraft until the appropriate Medical Examiner or
Coroner can retrieve the body
CONTINUES TO NEXT PAGE
Termination of Resuscitation
During Transport
b. Fixed-wing aircraft:
i. Proceed to the destination airport
ii. The body will be left inside the aircraft until the appropriate Medical Examiner or
Coroner can retrieve the body
c. Ground ambulance:
i. The crew should pull over at the next available safe location and contact 911 to
advise there was a death in the vehicle
ii. The Medical Examiner or Coroner will determine the appropriate rendezvous
location to retrieve the body (e.g., current location or proceeding to the receiving
hospital)
5. In all cases of resuscitation was terminated during transport, the Medical Examiner or Coroner will
be immediately notified.
a. Be prepared to give the following details:
i. Time resuscitation was terminated
ii. GPS coordinates when resuscitation was terminated
iii. Name of patient and/or other identifying data
iv. Life Flight Network Incident Run Number
v. Names of Flight Crew terminating resuscitation
vi. Location (city/county/state) where patient was picked-up
vii. Name of hospital or agency that transferred patient care to us
viii. Name of hospital security officer accepting patient’s valuables, if applicable

Parameter — Normal Value — Definition
Cardiac Index — 2.5 - 4 L/min — Cardiac output adjusted for body size
Cardiac Output (CO) — 4 - 8 L/min — Blood ejected from the heart into systemic circulation per minute
Central Venous Pressure — 0 - 8 mmHg — Reflects filling pressure of RV and mean pressure of systemic veins
Coronary Artery Perfusion Pressure — 60 – 80 mm Hg — The pressure gradient that drives blood flow through the coronary arteries
Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP) — 70 - 105 mmHg — The average pressure in a person's arteries during one cardiac cycle
Mean PA Pressure — 9 -16 mmHg — The average pressure in the arteries leading from the heart to lungs
Pulmonary Capillary Wedge Pressure (PCWP) — 5 - 12 mmhg — Reflects filling pressure of LV if no obstruction exists between catheter balloon tip and LV
Pulmonary Vascular Resistance — 155 - 255 dyn/sec/cm⁻⁵ — Resistance to RV ejection offered by pulmonary pressure. Reflects RV afterload.
Pulmponary Artery Pressure (PAP) — 15 - 25 mmhg; 6 - 12 mmHg — Reflects RV afterload & LV preload
Right Atrial Pressure — 2 - 6 mmHg — The blood pressure in the right atrium of the heart
Stroke Volume — 60 - 135 — The amount of blood ejected from the heart's left ventricle with each heartbeat
Systemic Vascular Resistance — 800 - 1200 dyn/sec/cm⁻⁵ — Resistance to LV ejection offered by aortic pressure. Reflects LV afterload.

10.06b EMS VAN Tool
• Arm Drift:
o If there is no arm drift, the patient is considered VAN negative, and no further testing is
done
o If the arm drift is positive, proceed to VAN testing
• Vision:
o With the patient looking at your nose, test vision in all 4 quadrants by holding up your
hand sequentially in each quadrant (right upper, right lower, left upper, left lower).
o Ask the patient to count how many fingers you are holding up (vary number in each
quadrant)
o Have the patient track your finger with their eyes, moving it left to right then right to left
and ask if they have double vision
o Failure to count fingers correctly or presence of double vision is considered positive
CONTINUES TO NEXT PAGE
Stroke Scales
• Aphasia:
o Have the patient name two objects (e.g., point to watch, hold up a pen, hold up your
phone).
o Have them repeat a statement (already done under Speech in the FAST exam). Have the
patient follow two commands: “close your eyes” and “make a fist”
o Failure to identify the two objects, repeat a statement or follow both commands is
considered positive
• Neglect:
o Look at patient’s eyes for forced gaze, looking persistently to right or left
o Then with patient’s eyes closed, touch their right arm, then left arm, then both arms.
o With each touch, have patient identify which arm you are touching
o The presence of forced gaze or inability to identify which arm is being touched is
considered positive
• Scoring VAN
o No arm weakness = VAN negative
o Arm weakness, but VAN tests all normal or negative = VAN negative
o Arm weakness and any one VAN test positive = VAN positive

▪ All pediatric push doses of epinephrine should be dosed and documented in mL/kg
▪ Epinephrine, norepinephrine, dopamine, fentanyl, and midazolam infusions should
be weight based for all pediatric patients regardless of weight.
▪ Contact receiving physician for pediatric ICU patients
o Pain Management
▪ Ketamine dose updated to 0.1 – 0.2 mg/kg
o Sedation: Post-Intubation
▪ Clarified that CPOT scores should not be documented for chemically paralyzed
patients

doses.indication:
• Pain Management
• Sepsis
• Fever
• Altitude Related
Emergencies
• Ischemic Stroke
• Post-ROSC
• Management
• Blood Product
Administration
doses.adult:
1000 mg IV over 15 minutes
• May repeat q 6 hours
doses.pediatric:
15 mg/kg IV over 15 minutes
• May repeat q 6 hours
• If ≥ 13 years and/or ≥ 50 kg,
utilize adult dose
• Max single dose of 750 mg

info.Mechanism of Action: Although not fully elucidated, the analgesic effects are believed to be due to activation of descending serotonergic inhibitory pathways in the CNS. Interactions with other nociceptive systems may be involved as well. Antipyresis is produced from inhibition of the hypothalamic heat- regulating center.
info.Contraindications: Hypersensitivity; Severe hepatic disease
info.Warnings / Precautions: Caution in patients with hepatic impairment; hypotension
info.Adverse Reactions: Hypotension with rapid administration; hepatotoxicity; nausea/vomiting; headache; thrombocytopenia

2. Maintenance dosing: Once initial control is achieved, administer 2 vials every 6 hours for up to 18
hours. Optimal dosing beyond 18 hours has not been established; however, treatment may be
continued if deemed necessary based on the patient's condition.
3. Antivenin dose reflects venom size rather than patient size; therefore, the FDA recommends the
same initial and subsequent doses for adult and pediatric patients regardless of age or weight.
4. Initiate therapy as soon as possible and preferably within 6 hours after a North American pit viper
bite in patients exhibiting any signs of envenomation. Clinicians are encouraged to contact their
local poison control center or clinical toxicologist for consultation when treating any envenomed
patient.
5. Although tourniquets are not recommended, antivenin therapy should be initiated prior to
tourniquet removal in patients who present with one in place. Tourniquet removal should only
occur after the patient is tolerating the full infusion rate without signs of anaphylaxis

1. Reconstituting and Administering Tenecteplase (TNKase)
a. Using the syringe, needle and Sterile Water supplied, draw the full 10 mL sterile water into
the syringe.
b. DO NOT use bacteriostatic water.
c. Inject the 10 mL sterile water into the TNKase, directing the stream of diluent into the
powder. There may be some foaming. Allow the vial to settle until bubbles dissipate.
d. Swirl the vial gently until contents are completely dissolved. DO NOT shake vial.
e. Final concentration is 50 mg/10 mL. Liquid should be clear and colorless/pale yellow.
f. Draw the appropriate volume Tenecteplase (TNKase) into the syringe. Leave extra solution
in the vial to avoid inadvertent overdosing.
g. Administer TNKase as a bolus over 5 seconds via a dedicated line.
h. Tenecteplase is incompatible with dextrose, so flush dextrose containing lines with NS
before and after administration of Tenecteplase.
